# Puck.Maths.Tests — LEG LEDGER

Machine-written by the assembly ledger when the leg gates ran. Every gate statement declares the legs it stands
on — every one of them a law case in LawRegistry.cs — and this file is those declarations read back. Never
hand-edited. Where legs share code, agreement proves everything EXCEPT the shared part; the registers below are
that gap, enumerated.

The gates check that the declarations are well formed and that a case's declaration matches the combinator it
ran. They cannot read the bodies the text describes: whether a leg called classical really shares no code is the
adversarial review's job, not this file's.

| algebra.clifford-exponential-scalar-square-domain | law: Default | structural | — | the acceptance boundary of Exponential, in both directions. Eleven in-domain bivectors are accepted, covering all three branches and the zero-generator scalar algebra: circular at (2,0,0) and (0,2,0), hyperbolic at (1,1,0), degenerate at (1,0,1), a mixed rotor at (3,0,0), the zero bivector, and the translator and screw generators at (3,0,1). Nine out-of-domain inputs are refused, and every refusal is an ArgumentException naming the 'bivector' parameter: a nonzero lane of grade zero, one, three or four; a grade-two element carrying an additional scalar or vector lane; and three genuine grade-two elements of (4,0,0) whose squares are not scalar (e12+e34, e13+e24, and an unequally weighted e12+e34) | — | — | — |
| algebra.clifford-exponential-scalar-square-domain | law: Default | classical | — | every accepted value, and the true exponential of the leading refused input | the versor identity: Reverse negates every grade-two blade, so for a bivector b the reverse of exp(b) is exp(−b) and exp(b)·Reverse(exp(b)) is exactly 1. That is a standard fact about the exponential of a grade-two element, read here off no implementation — it is applied through GeometricProduct and Reverse, which presented.clifford-reverse-anti-automorphism and the planar twins pin on their own | — | ENVELOPE: a MEASURED-PRECISION statement on the accepted side, since the branches round FixedQ4816.Sqrt, SinCos and Exp2. The worst residual over the eleven accepted cases is 4 raw on the scalar lane and 0 on every other, so the 16-raw ceiling is generous; it sits four thousand times below the 63942 raw by which the refused input's branch value misses |
| algebra.clifford-exponential-scalar-square-domain | law: Default | structural | — | the refusal of the non-simple bivector is WARRANTED, not over-strict. In (4,0,0) the blades e12 and e34 commute and are disjoint, so exp(e12+e34) is the product exp(e12)·exp(e34) of two IN-DOMAIN exponentials the same law accepts; the claim confirms that product carries a nonzero e1234 lane, which no branch of the scalar-square closed form can produce, and that it meets the versor identity to one raw. Reconstructing what the closed form would have returned for the same input — the circular branch on the square's scalar lane — gives a value that misses the versor identity by 63942 raw, more than two thirds of a unit, so the refused answer was wrong rather than imprecise | — | — | — |

The claim pins the choice in both directions at once: One under the tail [1,1] equals One under the tail [5,7], while the two descriptors that produced them stay unequal, so the modulus is distinguished exactly where it is stored and nowhere else. Degree is still part of identity — a degree-2 One is unequal to a degree-1 and a degree-3 One — as are default values, which equal only other defaults | — | — | — |
| algebra.monogenic-identity-is-tail-and-coordinates | law: Default | structural | — | the algebraic identities hold as VALUE equality, through the framework's own comparers rather than only coordinate by coordinate: Add(One, Zero) equals One, Zero equals the all-zero coordinate vector, Root equals MultiplyByRoot(One), a FixedQ4816 element times One lands back on an equal element, ProjectiveStep of two equal windows agrees while a window is unequal to its own successor, and a HashSet holding One both recognizes Add(One, Zero) as the same value and refuses a second read of One as a new one. Elements differing by one raw unit or one coordinate stay unequal. The digest is an Fnv1aHash fold over the carrier's own hash codes rather than a per-process-seeded one, so it is stable across runs and machines | — | — | — |

| binary-field.axioms-at-five-carriers | law: Default | structural | — | the field axioms hold BIT-FOR-BIT at all five carriers and at a modulus drawn from the operand stream: commutativity, associativity, distributivity, both identities, the annihilator, addition as its own inverse, Square as Multiply(a, a) — the wing's 'no separate squaring kernel on any tier' invariant stated as an observable — and Frobenius additivity, which is what licenses SquareRoot being repeated squaring. Everything here is EXACT: nothing rounds, saturates or approximates anywhere in the wing, so condition (B) does not arise at all — there is no rounding substrate for the two sides to share, and 'they agree because they round alike' is not a reading this statement admits | — | — | — |
| binary-field.axioms-at-five-carriers | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE, and it is the point of this case's shape: the axioms hold under ANY legal modulus, so agreement here pins the ARITHMETIC and never the modulus. A reduction that consistently used the wrong irreducible would satisfy every line above. What pins the modulus is binary-field.product-and-reduction-vs-oracle's published-constant and oracle legs and binary-field.irreducibility-vs-trial-division; this case is what catches a product wrong in a way no single oracle comparison would isolate — a non-associative fold, a distributivity break at a carry edge, an identity that moves at one degree | — | — | — |
| binary-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | the whole admission surface at all five carriers and five degrees each — degree one, degree two, half the width, one below the width and the width itself: Create succeeds, Degree and ReductionTail read back exactly what was passed, IsReduced answers correctly at One, at Zero, at the degree's all-ones mask and at t^degree, and Reduce(t^degree) is the ReductionTail. The degree == width row is the one the representation exists for: a degree-k modulus needs k + 1 bits and would not fit the carrier, which is why the leading term is implicit | — | — | — |
| binary-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | the refusal ladder, each row asserting the exception TYPE and the ParamName: an unsupported carrier (char and nuint, both of which satisfy the IBinaryInteger/IUnsignedNumber constraint and neither of which is one of the five fixed widths — nuint is eight bytes wide on this target, so it would otherwise look exactly like ulong to CarrierBitCount) is refused with NotSupportedException BEFORE the degree is looked at; a degree below one or above the carrier's width names 'degree'; an even tail — a zero constant term, where t divides the modulus and the quotient is not a field — names 'reductionTail'; a tail with a coefficient at or above the degree names 'reductionTail', and that check is SKIPPED at degree == width, where nothing can sit above it. FromModulus refuses the zero polynomial and the degree-zero constant with ArgumentOutOfRangeException naming 'modulus' — the same shared range rule Create runs, asserted EXACTLY so the ArgumentException base cannot stand in — and its carrier check still precedes the degree rules, so an unsupported carrier reports NotSupportedException from both factories | — | — | — |
| binary-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | FromModulus's two DERIVED refusals name 'modulus', the one parameter its caller supplied: a modulus whose degree exceeds the carrier's width throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException naming 'modulus', and a modulus with a zero constant term throws ArgumentException naming 'modulus'. The counterexample reads the offending name back rather than reporting a bare boolean. The same rows are what pins the two factories APART: Create's own degree and tail refusals still name 'degree' and 'reductionTail', so the shared validation core is reporting the name it was handed rather than one set of names having swallowed the other. This statement REPLACES the doc gap that pinned the leaked names; FromModulus's XML doc attributed both conditions to modulus all along, and the code now agrees with it | — | — | — |

The two top rows also carry a load-bearing structural fact: BinaryPolynomial's packed carrier tops out at degree 63, so Degree64 and Degree128 are reachable ONLY through Create, and the round-trip ladder below shows FromModulus reaching degree 63 and no further |
| binary-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | FromModulus round-trips the leading-term strip: for a committed ladder of degrees through 63 with odd tails, FromModulus of (t^degree + tail) reports that degree and that tail exactly. ENVELOPE: BinaryPolynomial's own packed-bits constructor and Bits reader are INPUTS here rather than subjects — this case could not catch either of them being wrong, so neither is cited, and both answer to polynomial.additive-group-and-accessors | — | — | — |
| binary-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | a DEFAULT-INITIALIZED field REFUSES its whole semantic surface with InvalidOperationException, at all five supported carriers and at an unassigned array element of each: One, Zero, Add, AddRegion, Divide, Exponentiate, Inverse, IsIrreducible, IsReduced, Multiply, MultiplyAccumulateRegion, Reduce, ScaleRegion, ScaleRegionInPlace, Square and SquareRoot, each named in the failure text so a member that quietly answers is reported as itself. Every one of these previously returned a PLAUSIBLE answer at degree zero — the truncated carryless product, an identity Reduce, an identity SquareRoot from a loop handed −1, and a successful Inverse(One) — none of which is arithmetic in GF(2^k). Degree and ReductionTail are deliberately outside the policy and still read zero, and this case asserts that the default value therefore stays comparable and that a CONSTRUCTED field is untouched: it answers, both identities read back, and record equality still reads the degree and the tail rather than any encoding of them. PRINTABILITY is asserted on ToString at both ends: a hand-written PrintMembers prints the degree and the tail alone, so a default value formats as its raw state instead of throwing from a guarded identity, and a constructed field renders no identity as if it were carried state | — | — | — |
| binary-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | the same refusal at an UNSUPPORTED carrier: default(BinaryField<char>) refuses Multiply, Add, Inverse, IsIrreducible and One with the SAME InvalidOperationException. That carrier has no constructed state at all — Create rejects it with NotSupportedException before the degree is read — so the uninitialized diagnosis is the only thing its default value can say, and the policy makes it say exactly what the five supported carriers say rather than reaching degree-independent members undiagnosed | — | — | — |
| binary-field.irreducibility-vs-trial-division | law: Default | classical | — | BinaryField<byte>.IsIrreducible at EVERY one of the 255 legal degree-1-through-8 moduli | Oracles.BinaryPolynomialIsIrreducible — exhaustive trial division by every polynomial of degree one through half the modulus's own, in BigInteger. The definition against the Ben-Or/Rabin criterion: the subject squares the indeterminate degree times and takes gcds of t^(2^i) + t against the modulus through a bespoke first Euclid step that never materializes the modulus, and the oracle just divides. Exhaustive rather than sampled, so this is a TOTAL statement over that whole range and not a probe. EXACT on both sides, so the substrate condition does not arise | — | — |
| binary-field.irreducibility-vs-trial-division | law: Default | classical | — | the count of constructible irreducible moduli the sweep above finds at each degree from one through eight | Subjects.BinaryIrreducibleCounts — 2, 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18, 30 — with the degree-one entry taken as one | — | OEIS A001037, the number of monic irreducible polynomials of each degree over GF(2) — Gauss's necklace count, an external property of the ring itself. The published degree-one entry is 2 and the sweep can only find 1, because t has a zero constant term and Create refuses it; every irreducible of degree two or above has a non-zero constant term, so those rows are the published values unchanged. An implementation that is self-consistently wrong still cannot reproduce a published property of GF(2)[t]. The table is the binary-polynomial family's own, reused rather than copied |
| binary-field.irreducibility-vs-trial-division | law: Default | classical | — | IsIrreducible() at all five catalog fields | true at every one | — | the standard minimum-weight irreducibles at degrees 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128, tabulated in src/Puck.Maths/FiniteFields/README.md. The catalog deliberately does NOT validate irreducibility at construction — the README says the constants are not trusted on their word and expect an external gate — and Post's binary-field stage re-proves the same five at run time |
| binary-field.irreducibility-vs-trial-division | law: Default | classical | — | IsIrreducible() at t^degree + 1 for degree 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128 | false at every one | — | the Frobenius identity in characteristic two: t^(2^k) + 1 = (t + 1)^(2^k), so the modulus is a perfect power and maximally reducible. ENVELOPE: this is the ONLY negative statement this suite makes at degrees 32, 64 and 128 — the trial-division oracle's divisor space doubles with every degree and is out of reach above the teens, so the positive statement at the wide degrees rests on the published constants plus Post's binary-field stage, and deep.binary-field-irreducible-census is where the exhaustive agreement is carried further |
| binary-field.irreducibility-vs-trial-division | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE on a branch that cannot be falsified, measured rather than assumed: the kernel's closing `power == indeterminate` test — Rabin's t^(2^degree) ≡ t condition — is UNREACHABLE as a decision, because the loop above it runs the STRENGTHENED Ben-Or form over every exponent through half the degree, and every reducible modulus has an irreducible factor of degree at most half its own, so the greatest-common-divisor arm has already returned false by the time that test is read. Replacing it with a bare `true` moves no answer over the 255 moduli here or the 8190 the binary-polynomial family sweeps; the only legal degree-one modulus is t + 1, which is irreducible either way. This law pins the DECISION, not that closing guard, and says so rather than implying the guard is covered | — | — | — |

ENVELOPE: this second derivation runs at the two narrow catalog degrees at Default and at all five at deep.binary-field-multiplicative-group; at degrees 32, 64 and 128 the certificate leg above is what stands, and it is complete for the value even though it is not a second derivation of it | — | — |

ENVELOPE: degree 128 has NO row, because 2^128 − 1 does not fit the ulong exponent Exponentiate takes. A dropped leading term, a Split that returned its value unshifted, or a fold loop unrolled to one pass all diverge here on the first drawn modulus that needs a second pass. ENVELOPE, measured rather than assumed: ReduceWide's low mask is deliberately built by right-shifting all-ones instead of as (1 << degree) − 1, and rebuilding it the second way is NOT falsifiable through the public surface, because Split short-circuits at degree == width and returns before the mask is read — the mutation is inert at every carrier. ENVELOPE: at degree == width the t^degree probe is unrepresentable in the carrier and is not made. ENVELOPE: in Domains.Vectors' single-lane edge phase every other lane is cleared, so a 128-bit operand assembled from two lanes carries a zero half there and the drawn modulus lands on degree 1, tail 1 — GF(2), which the wing builds on every cyclic-incidence run and is a real instantiation rather than a degenerate one | — | — | — |

Each length row additionally requires the element one past the region to be untouched | — | — | — |

At a catalog field the statement would say nothing, because degree equals width there and every packed value is already reduced. It is the wing's one region member outside the scaling ladder, and this is the statement that would catch it acquiring a reduction | — | — | — |
| binary-field.regions-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the length-mismatch refusal is an ArgumentOutOfRangeException naming the PUBLIC parameter 'source', at all three validating members and in BOTH directions of mismatch — a shorter source and a longer one — and it lands before anything is written: the eight-element buffer carries distinct content and every element is compared back after each refused call. The name is intentional rather than inherited: the refusal is thrown explicitly, because the throw helper it used to run captured the caller-argument expression of ValidateRegion's first argument and reported the literal string 'source.Length', which is a property expression and not a parameter of any public member. This statement REPLACES the doc gap that pinned that string; the three members' XML docs now name source, and the shifted-overlap refusal already did | — | — | — |
| binary-field.wide-degree-irreducibility-certificates | law: Default | classical | — | BinaryField<T>.IsIrreducible at degrees 32, 64 and 128 — the Ben-Or/Rabin criterion in BinaryFieldKernels — on the catalog modulus at each degree and on the first FURTHER modulus the subject accepts there, taken over the 128-bit carrier | an exact multiplicative-ORDER certificate in BigInteger: an element a of the quotient ring with a^(2^d − 1) = 1 and a^((2^d − 1)/p) not 1 at every prime p dividing 2^d − 1. Its order is then 2^d − 1 EXACTLY, so its powers are that many distinct units of a ring holding 2^d elements one of which is zero — every non-zero element therefore inverts, the quotient IS a field, and the modulus is irreducible. A COMPLETE proof and not a probe, and it shares nothing with the subject: no Frobenius exponentiation, no greatest common divisor, no carrier, no split, no reduction tail folded the subject's way — only Oracles.BinaryFieldProduct and a square-and-multiply schedule over BigInteger. This is the statement the wide degrees never had: trial division, the oracle every narrow irreducibility law answers to, has a divisor space that doubles with the degree and cannot be run at 32 at all | — | the prime divisors are the published Fermat-number factorizations, 2^32 + 1 = 641 x 6700417 and 2^64 + 1 = 274177 x 67280421310721; the catalog tails 0x8D, 0x1B and 0x87 are the standard minimum-weight irreducibles tabulated in src/Puck.Maths/FiniteFields/README.md. NEITHER is trusted here — the last structural leg of this case re-multiplies every factorization and re-proves every factor prime before a certificate reads it, and the tails are decided by the certificate rather than accepted |

Each modulus is the carryless PRODUCT of two non-constant polynomials, formed by Oracles.CarrylessProduct in BigInteger, so the reference verdict follows from how the operand was built and no decision procedure is consulted anywhere. Before a row is used the claim body requires the product to have landed on the intended degree with a non-zero constant term, so a construction that silently degenerated reddens the case rather than emptying it. FNV-1a is DEFINED by its offset basis, its prime and its exclusive-or-then-multiply recurrence, so any reference computed inside this suite would be the implementation restated and would prove nothing about it; the published vectors are the only evidence available here that is not a second spelling of the subject. The empty-span row is the load-bearing one — an accumulator that failed to prime itself returns zero there and the offset basis nowhere — and the three single-character rows differ only in the byte folded, so a fold that ignored its input agrees with none of them. |

The scaling branch is reached only from here: mass-properties.volumes-vs-oracle calls the helper exclusively at a zero fraction bit count, and Physics's nonzero-shift caller has no law of its own. | Oracles.RoundedRational — the same rational taken independently, scaling by a BigInteger.Pow multiply rather than a shift and deciding the tie by doubling the remainder against the divisor rather than comparing it with the distance to the next multiple | — | — |
| core.rust-port-emitters-are-pure-and-live | law: Default | structural | — | both emitters are PURE: each produces byte-identical text on two calls, and running one between two calls of the other does not disturb it. That is the property the type's own remarks claim — no wall clock, no unseeded source, an unchanged host giving byte-identical output every run — and it is the property a generated artifact committed to the tree depends on, since a drifting emitter makes every regeneration a spurious diff. A shared StringBuilder, a static cursor or a re-seeded generator all fail it. | — | — | — |
| core.rust-port-emitters-are-pure-and-live | law: Default | structural | — | the emitted text carries the LIVE values it claims to read: FixedQ4816.Atan2HalfPiQ61 and PiQ61 appear in the generated source as the invariant decimals the type currently holds, and the emitted vector file carries the raw value the live FixedQ4816.Sin returns for one. That is the whole design claim this file makes for itself — every table and coefficient read from the live type by NAME rather than transcribed — so a constant referenced by the wrong name, or a vector file that emitted its inputs without the host's answers, stops satisfying it. | — | — | — |
| core.rust-port-emitters-are-pure-and-live | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE, and it is the reason this is a purity-and-transcription law rather than a port-agreement one: NOTHING here executes the emitted Rust or compares it against the committed artifact, so this law says nothing about whether the ported algorithm still agrees with its host bit for bit. That statement needs the emitted text compiled and run against known-answer vectors, which no gate in this repository performs today — the stage that compared emitted text against what is committed left the build with Puck.Post, and the type's own remarks say so. OWED: a runner that regenerates and diffs, or that executes the port. Until one exists, drift in the PORT is caught only by a human regenerating and reading the diff, and only drift in the emitter's own determinism and constant references is caught here. | — | — | — |

MIRROR of unit-fraction32.text-vs-oracle; this is the family's heaviest law (thirty-three-digit BigInteger rationals per case) and Deep is where it is paid for | — | — |

MIRROR at exhaustive fraction coverage | — | — |

The counts are hand-derived from the two kernels and compared against OBSERVED refusals, so a refusal that moved by one raw fails the case | — | — | — |

| directed-rounding.ceiling-magnitude-is-least-upper-bound | law: Default | classical | — | FixedDirectedRounding.TryCeilingMagnitude (public, both the two- and the three-component overload — one CoverRef credits both, since resolution is by name) — the direction and tightness of the rounded-up Euclidean norm at the components' own scale, over the FULL signed range of every component (a magnitude is non-negative whatever the signs are, which is why these two members alone in the family admit negative operands) | Oracles.CeilingIntegerRoot over the exact sum of squares in BigInteger — a bracketed search on one exact squaring, against the subject's floor root plus a settle. result^2 >= radicand AND (result-1)^2 < radicand are both asserted | — | — |
| directed-rounding.ceiling-magnitude-is-least-upper-bound | law: Default | structural | — | The directed norm never falls BELOW FixedVectorMath.TryMagnitude's round-to-nearest norm at the same components — the round-to-nearest sibling is left exactly as it was, and this is the one relation between them the family promises. Three squared 64-bit raws total at most 3*2^126, inside UInt128, so the sum is exact and no preconditioning is involved; the root can still leave the raw, which is refused with the output at zero | — | — | — |
| directed-rounding.ceiling-product-is-least-upper-bound | law: Default | classical | — | FixedDirectedRounding.TryCeilingProduct (public) — the direction and tightness of the rounded-up mixed-scale product over non-negative operands and every fraction bit count in [0, 64] | Oracles.CeilingRational — the exact rational value formed in BigInteger and ceilinged as a floor plus a remainder test, deliberately NOT as (n + d - 1)/d, which is the shape a fixed-width kernel reaches for and the shape that overflows. The law asserts result*denominator >= numerator AND (result-1)*denominator < numerator, then equality with the oracle | — | — |
| directed-rounding.ceiling-product-is-least-upper-bound | law: Default | structural | — | The refuse/succeed verdict is a biconditional: the subject's only overflow path is a left shift whose true magnitude passes 2^128, which puts the exact value far past the signed 64-bit raw, so declining and not-representable coincide. A refusal leaves the output at zero | — | — | — |
| directed-rounding.ceiling-product-sum-is-least-upper-bound | law: Default | classical | — | FixedDirectedRounding.TryCeilingProductSum (public) — the direction and tightness of the rounded-up a*b + addend over non-negative operands at three independent scales, with both terms lifted by a LOSSLESS left shift onto the finer of the two scales so the addition is exact and only the narrowing rounds | Oracles.CeilingRational over the exact rational (a*b*2^(m-p) + addend*2^(m-q)) * 2^(fractionBitsOut - m), computed in BigInteger with no width limit at all | — | — |
| directed-rounding.ceiling-product-sum-is-least-upper-bound | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE, modelled exactly rather than tolerated: each lifted term must fit 127 bits, not UInt128's full 128, BECAUSE the two are then added and two 128-bit terms need a 129th bit the accumulator does not have. Where either term needs the 128th bit the subject REFUSES — a declined answer, never a wrong one, and one that can decline a value the raw could have held. The law computes both terms exactly and demands an answer only inside that budget, so a subject that widened the budget (and wrapped) or narrowed it (and declined more) would both fail | — | — | — |
| directed-rounding.ceiling-quotient-is-least-upper-bound | law: Default | classical | — | FixedDirectedRounding.TryCeilingQuotient (public) — the direction and tightness of the rounded-up mixed-scale quotient over a non-negative dividend, a strictly positive divisor and every fraction bit count in [0, 64] | Oracles.CeilingRational over the exact rational numerator*2^e / denominator. The subject scales the dividend when that exponent is non-negative and the DIVISOR when it is negative, so neither side is rounded before the single division; the oracle keeps both as an exact fraction and never shifts anything | — | — |
| directed-rounding.ceiling-quotient-is-least-upper-bound | law: Default | structural | — | Both scaling extremes are answered rather than declined, and the law pins that: an oversized dividend forces a quotient of at least 2^65, past the raw, so refusal there IS the representability verdict; an oversized divisor puts the exact ratio strictly inside (0, 1), whose ceiling is exactly one, and the subject returns one rather than refusing. The verdict is therefore a biconditional against representability alone. directed-rounding.negative-operands-refuse pins the 1/3 witness where a nearest-rounding kernel would answer zero | — | — | — |
| directed-rounding.ceiling-square-root-is-least-upper-bound | law: Default | classical | — | FixedDirectedRounding.TryCeilingSquareRoot (public) — the DIRECTION and the TIGHTNESS of the rounded-up square root at every output fraction bit count in [0, 64], over radicands folded onto the non-negative half of the carrier by one logical shift (which preserves the raw's own bit pattern, so the committed edge battery still lands on the seams) | Oracles.CeilingIntegerRoot — a bracketed integer search, doubling to a bracket and bisecting it, whose only predicate is one exact squaring; no square root is ever taken. The subject instead takes a floor root and carries it up when the radicand is not a perfect square. The law asserts result^2 >= radicand AND (result-1)^2 < radicand, so it is the LEAST representable upper bound, not merely near the true root — a kernel that rounded to nearest and added one unit in the last place fails the second half | — | — |
| directed-rounding.ceiling-square-root-is-least-upper-bound | law: Default | structural | — | The refuse/succeed verdict is a biconditional here, not an envelope: the subject declines exactly when the scaled radicand leaves UInt128 or the root leaves the raw, and a radicand at or past 2^128 forces a root at or past 2^64, which cannot fit the raw either — so the two refusal conditions coincide and no conservative corner exists. A refusal must leave the output at zero, asserted against the subject directly | — | — | — |
| directed-rounding.negative-operands-refuse | law: Default | structural | — | Every arithmetic member of the directed-up family refuses a negative operand — and TryCeilingQuotient a zero or negative divisor, and TryCeilingSquareRoot a negative fraction bit count — returning false with its output at zero, rather than choosing silently between 'up' meaning toward positive infinity and 'up' meaning away from zero. The two magnitude overloads are the deliberate exception and are checked to ACCEPT negative components, answering the exact 5 for (-3,-4). The claim also pins the discriminating witness for the whole family: the exact ratio 1/3 at zero output fraction bits must answer 1, where a kernel that quietly rounded to nearest would answer 0 and pass every proximity check | — | — | — |
| dual.additive-group-exact | law: Default | classical | — | FixedDual<FixedQ4816>.op_Addition, both parts | Oracles.WrapToRaw of the exact componentwise BigInteger sum, inline in Subjects.DualAdditiveGroupExact — exact both sides | — | — |

| dual.additive-group-exact | law: Default | structural | — | the positional constructor and the two part readers round-trip at every swept raw, so a swapped positional order fails here rather than hiding inside a symmetric product | — | — | — |
| dual.additive-group-exact | law: Default | structural | — | AdditiveIdentity is default(FixedDual<FixedQ4816>), is a two-sided identity for op_Addition, and a − a is exactly it, at every swept raw including both two's-complement extremes | — | — | — |

InitialResponse is not swept: CompilePropagator's guard-scale roundings never depend on it. | — | — | — |

THIS law folds frequency to [0.5, 8] Hz rather than the full (0, 100] Hz authoring band (the upper bound avoids many-cycle phase-rounding divergence over one second at 240 one-tick steps; the lower bound avoids a near-zero decay rate where both sides' rounding noise dominates a genuinely tiny signal) and nudges the damping ratio off the near-critical band \|zeta-1\| < 1/6 (there the overdamped closed form divides two nearly-equal decay rates by a near-zero sigma, a genuinely different numerical regime this generic bound is not shaped to cover) |

| extension-field.batch-inverse-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the in-place round trip: Multiply(values[i], original[i]) is One for every i of every batch, so a peel-off that mixed two positions is caught POSITIONALLY rather than only in aggregate | — | — | — |

| extension-field.batch-inverse-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | an EMPTY span returns without throwing and without writing, which the early return at QuadraticExtensionField64.cs:90 is the whole of | — | — | — |

The ELEMENT-level arithmetic is what the swept cases own | — | — | — |

Exact on both sides, so (B) is vacuous; what the leg pins is the character decision and the walk together | — | — |
| extension-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | classical | — | SmallestNonSquare at all thirteen ladder primes | the Subjects.ExtensionPrime ladder's own declared second field — 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 5, 3, 3, 2, 3, 11, 3, 3 at the moduli 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 97, 257, 65537, 1000003, 998244353, 2013265921, 2147483647 and 2^61 − 1 | — | hand-derived from quadratic reciprocity and the supplementary law that 2 is a residue exactly at p ≡ ±1 (mod 8); the derivation for every entry is written out in the campaign spec. Deliberately a SECOND reference beside leg 1: the table is what a reference wrong in the same way as the subject would still have to agree with, and a wrong table fails the case rather than passing it. The failure message says which way to correct — where the Euler-criterion reference agrees with the subject, the TABLE is what is wrong |
| extension-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | classical | — | the MINIMALITY the member's name claims | Oracles.PrimeFieldCharacter at every candidate strictly between two and the returned value — each must be a residue, never a non-residue — and BigInteger.ModPow of the returned value at (p − 1)/2 must be exactly p − 1 rather than merely not one. Without this leg the walk could return any non-residue at all and still pass leg 1, and a composite modulus could reach the character undetected | — | — |
| extension-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | CreateCanonical is Create over the smallest non-square: its NonSquare equals the ladder's declared value, its BaseField equals the field it was handed, and the whole record equals Create(field, that value). CreateCanonical bypasses Create's guard by calling the private constructor (QuadraticExtensionField64.cs:54-55), so that it lands on the same object is a statement rather than a wiring fact | — | — | — |
| extension-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | classical | — | Create's ACCEPT/REFUSE decision, exhaustively over every reduced value in [1, p) at the six ladder primes at or below 97 and over a fixed square ladder plus the declared non-square above them | Oracles.PrimeFieldCharacter: Create must throw ArgumentException naming the parameter nonSquare exactly where the character is +1, and must succeed with NonSquare and BaseField reading back verbatim exactly where it is −1. The case fails on a wrong REFUSAL as readily as on a wrong acceptance | — | — |
| extension-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | Create REFUSES the literal zero with ArgumentException naming nonSquare, at every ladder prime — the arm LegendreCharacter's own zero short-circuit is the whole of, and the one value where the folding described in the reduced-generator row below does not apply | — | — | — |
| extension-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | the REDUCED-GENERATOR bound, enforced ahead of the character test and stated at every ladder prime: the modulus itself, twice the modulus, the modulus plus the declared non-square, and ulong.MaxValue are each refused with ArgumentOutOfRangeException naming nonSquare. The modulus row is the one with teeth — LegendreCharacter folds an unreduced argument through ScaledResidueRing64.Encode and reports the resulting zero power as −1 rather than 0 (PrimeField64.cs:391-397), so the character alone would ADMIT p and hand back F_p[t]/(t²), the dual numbers. The other rows are what keep record equality meaning 'the supplied reduced generator agrees': d and d + p can no longer become two unequal descriptors of one extension. This statement REPLACES the doc gap that pinned the old acceptance | — | — | — |
| extension-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | the DEFINING field invariant, by exhaustion at the ladder primes 3, 5, 7, 11 and 13 and over EVERY generator Create accepts at each: only the zero element has a vanishing Norm, every non-zero element has one, and Multiply(element, Inverse(element)) is One. This is precisely the statement the admitted-modulus quotient failed — its non-zero surd (0, 1) had norm zero and no inverse — so it is what the bound above is worth, measured rather than argued. ENVELOPE: quadratic in the modulus and run once per accepted generator, so it stops at 13; the primes above it are covered by the accept/refuse decision and by this family's arithmetic cases, which never reach a descriptor the bound would have caught | — | — | — |
| extension-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | every factory names the DESCRIPTOR when it was handed one that names no field: Create, CreateCanonical and SmallestNonSquare each refuse a default-initialized baseField with ArgumentException naming 'baseField', ahead of any generator work. Without it the reduced bound would compare against a zero modulus and blame nonSquare for a base-field mistake | — | — | — |
| extension-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | the DEFAULT EXTENSION is its own descriptor rather than a wrapper the base field's guard happens to cover, and it is stated separately: One, Zero, Add, Subtract, Negate, Multiply, Inverse, Pow, Norm, Trace, Frobenius, FromBase and BatchInverse at length zero and length three all refuse with InvalidOperationException, at `default` and at an unassigned array element alike, each row named in the failure text. Without the extension's own guard, coordinate addition and negation would inherit unreduced base-field arithmetic while the product and inverse paths failed incidentally on a zero modulus — the same split the prime field carried. BaseField and NonSquare stay outside the policy and read the uninitialized state, which is what this case asserts equality against — and PRINTABILITY is asserted on ToString itself: a hand-written PrintMembers prints the base field and the non-square alone, so a default value formats as its raw state, nested default base field included, instead of throwing from a guarded identity with the failure misattributed to the PRIME field whose One prints first in the synthesized walk | — | — | — |
| extension-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | extension identity: two extensions are equal exactly when both the base field and the non-square agree — equal at the same pair, unequal at two distinct non-squares of one prime (3 and 5 over F_7, whose residues are 1, 2 and 4), and unequal at one non-square SHARED by two primes (6, the least value outside the residues of both F_7 and F_11; 3 will not serve, because it is 5² modulo eleven and Create rightly refuses it there) | — | — | — |
| extension-field.construction-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE: this case consumes no operand domain and advances no frontier counter — its statement is quantified over the declared prime ladder and, at or below 97, over each field's whole residue set, which is exhaustion rather than sampling | — | — | — |
| extension-field.inverse-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | QuadraticExtensionField64.Inverse — the conjugate divided by the norm, whose one base-field inversion is PrimeField64.Inverse = value^(p − 2) run in ScaledResidueRing64's Montgomery form (QuadraticExtensionField64.cs:136-143, PrimeField64.cs:382-386) | Oracles.ModularInverse of the reference norm by the EXTENDED EUCLIDEAN algorithm, lifted to the pair (a·n⁻¹ mod p, (p − b·n⁻¹) mod p) in BigInteger. Euclid is a different THEOREM from Fermat and the reference never enters Montgomery form, so neither the algorithm nor the representation is shared. Exact on both sides — (B) is vacuous | — | — |
| extension-field.inverse-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the round trip: Multiply(x, Inverse(x)) is One at every swept non-zero element of every lean ladder prime, which is the statement a wrong norm and a wrong conjugate cannot both survive | — | — | — |
| extension-field.inverse-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | Inverse is an INVOLUTION — Inverse(Inverse(x)) == x — and it fixes One | — | — | — |
| extension-field.inverse-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the refusal: Inverse(Zero) throws DivideByZeroException, raised by PrimeField64.Inverse through the vanishing norm. ENVELOPE: in a genuine field Zero is the ONLY element whose norm vanishes, so the throwing arm is reached by exactly one operand — which the claim body visits explicitly on every iteration whatever the domain drew, rather than waiting for the sweep to supply it | — | — | — |
| extension-field.inverse-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE: the operand fold reduces every raw before it reaches the type, and the swept element is replaced by One where the fold lands on Zero, so the VALUE statement runs over every other element and the zero case is the refusal above | — | — | — |

| extension-field.norm-trace-frobenius-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | QuadraticExtensionField64.Norm's MULTIPLICATIVITY — N(x·y) against N(x)·N(y) | the unbounded BigInteger product of the two reference norms reduced once, inline in Subjects.ExtensionNormTraceFrobeniusExact. | extension-field.norm-trace-frobenius-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | QuadraticExtensionField64.Trace | (2a) mod p formed unbounded in BigInteger and reduced once, inline in the same claim. The RULE is a single doubling on both sides and there is no second derivation of it; what this leg buys is the reduction policy — the subject's conditional fold sum >= Modulus against the reference's unbounded double and one remainder — and it says so rather than claiming more | — | — |
| extension-field.norm-trace-frobenius-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | QuadraticExtensionField64.Frobenius | the pair (a, (p − b) mod p) formed in BigInteger, inline in the same claim — the conjugate reached without the subject's PrimeField64.Negate branch | — | — |
| extension-field.norm-trace-frobenius-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the CHARACTERISTIC EQUATION: Multiply(x, x) equals Subtract(Multiply(FromBase(Trace(x)), x), FromBase(Norm(x))) at every swept element. | extension-field.norm-trace-frobenius-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the defining equations of the conjugation: Multiply(x, Frobenius(x)) equals FromBase(Norm(x)) and Add(x, Frobenius(x)) equals FromBase(Trace(x)) | — | — | — |
| extension-field.norm-trace-frobenius-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | Frobenius is an INVOLUTION and its fixed set is EXACTLY the base field: Frobenius(Frobenius(x)) == x everywhere, and Frobenius(x) == x if and only if x.B is zero. The 'exactly' half holds because p is odd, so b and −b differ for every non-zero b — the one place this family's characteristic enters a statement, and the half that catches a Frobenius that is the identity map | — | — | — |
| extension-field.norm-trace-frobenius-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | Frobenius is a ring AUTOMORPHISM on the swept pair: it carries sums to sums and products to products | — | — | — |
| extension-field.norm-trace-frobenius-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE: as in extension-field.ring-vs-oracle, the operand fold reduces every raw before it reaches the type and the small ladder primes are degenerate under the edge battery | — | — | — |

| extension-field.pow-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | QuadraticExtensionField64.Pow at the exponent p itself, at all three lean primes — sixty-one extension squarings at the top of the ladder, the deepest chain the type reaches in this suite | the pair (a, (p − b) mod p) formed in BigInteger: the p-power map IS the conjugation, because d is a non-square and so d^((p − 1)/2) is −1. | extension-field.pow-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the group order: Pow(x, p² − 1) is One at every swept non-zero element of every LADDER PRIME BELOW 2³², the order of F_{p²}'s multiplicative group. ENVELOPE: p² − 1 leaves ulong above 2³², so the 61-bit ladder entry is pinned by the p-power and (p + 1)-power legs instead of by this one — stated rather than left as a silent gap | — | — | — |
| extension-field.pow-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the exponent poles the doc names: Pow(x, 0) is One for EVERY x including Zero, Pow(x, 1) is x, and Pow(Zero, e) is Zero at a non-zero ladder exponent | — | — | — |
| extension-field.pow-vs-oracle | law: Default | shared-substrate | shared-exact-kernel | Pow at the exponents 0 through 8 | the same number of iterated Multiply calls on the same element | QuadraticExtensionField64.Multiply — the IDENTICAL member on both sides, so this leg pins the SCHEDULE and never the product. | extension-field.product-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | QuadraticExtensionField64.Multiply at the 61-bit ladder prime 2⁶¹ − 1, over the house FOUR-OPERAND edge battery — every element component drawn from the committed edge set independently, which the width-2 lane stream in extension-field.ring-vs-oracle does not do | Oracles.PrimeFieldPolynomialProduct at tail [p − d, 0] — the same shared-nothing schoolbook route. Exact on both sides, so (B) drops out | — | — |
| extension-field.product-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the raw carriage is lossless in BOTH directions: every reduced component is below PrimeField64.MaximumModulus = 2⁶², so Subjects.ExtensionResidue lands inside the non-negative longs the BinaryElemOp shape carries and the returned coordinates cast back without wrapping. No sign or width policy sits between the law and the kernel | — | — | — |
| extension-field.product-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE: this law's edge battery runs at ONE modulus — the 61-bit one, where the base products actually fill the UInt128 reduction and where the edge set spreads across the most residues. The other ladder entries are swept by extension-field.ring-vs-oracle instead, on its own key | — | — | — |
| extension-field.ring-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | QuadraticExtensionField64.Multiply — five reduced base-field products with the square of the root folded back to the non-square (QuadraticExtensionField64.cs:148-157), at the three lean ladder primes 7, 1_000_003 and 2^61 − 1 | Oracles.PrimeFieldPolynomialProduct at tail [p − d, 0] — SCHOOLBOOK multiplication into a three-coefficient wide array followed by top-down reduction against the monic tail, in BigInteger. No closed pair formula anywhere on the reference side, and its own remark states no Montgomery form, no Barrett reduction, no field descriptor (Oracles.cs:1618-1619). Both sides EXACT, so condition (B) drops out entirely — there is no rounding substrate to share — and what agreement pins is purely the reduction policy | — | — |
| extension-field.ring-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | QuadraticExtensionField64.Add, Subtract and Negate — coordinate-wise through PrimeField64's three conditional folds | the unbounded BigInteger sum, difference and negation reduced ONCE by ((x % p) + p) % p, inline in Subjects.ExtensionRingExact. The reference never branches where the subject's carrier forces it to: PrimeField64.Add tests sum >= Modulus, Subtract tests left >= right, Negate special-cases zero. Exact on both sides, so (B) is vacuous | — | — |
| extension-field.ring-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | QuadraticExtensionField64.FromBase as the ring embedding of F_p | the BigInteger base sum and base product of the two lifted coordinates, inline in the same claim — the lift of a sum is the sum of the lifts and likewise for products, with both base values re-formed in arbitrary width rather than through PrimeField64 | — | — |
| extension-field.ring-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the Element positional constructor and its two readers round-trip at every swept pair BEFORE anything else reads them, and the product's two coordinates are compared against the polynomial reference's coefficient 0 and coefficient 1 SEPARATELY — the two are computed by different formulas, so a swapped constructor argument or a swapped reader reddens the multiply comparison rather than cancelling | — | — | — |
| extension-field.ring-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the ring axioms the type declares: Zero is (0, 0) and a two-sided additive identity, One is (1, 0) and a two-sided multiplicative identity, Negate is the additive inverse, and Subtract(x, y) equals Add(x, Negate(y)) at every swept pair | — | — | — |
| extension-field.ring-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE: the operand fold Subjects.ExtensionResidue reduces every sampled raw into [0, p) before it reaches the type, so this law says NOTHING about the unreduced-operand behaviour the members' docs decline to guard. ENVELOPE: at p = 7 the twenty-four committed edge raws collapse onto seven residues, so the small end of the ladder is degenerate by construction and the 61-bit entry is where the edge battery actually spreads | — | — | — |
| fft.convolution-aliasing-contract | law: Default | structural | — | Convolve(x, x, destination) with exact same-span operands is bit-identical to Convolve(copy(x), copy(x), destination) at lengths 1 through 256. Partial operand overlap is refused naming right, and any destination overlap is refused naming destination; both refusals occur before either operand changes. This pins the dedicated one-forward self-convolution path and the zero-allocation overlap boundary independently of the bounded arithmetic accuracy statement in fft.convolution-vs-oracle-bound. | — | — | — |
| fft.convolution-vs-oracle-bound | law: Default | classical | — | FixedFourierTransform.Convolve at lengths 1 through 256 over Pcg32XshRr-seeded complex operands in raw [-2^16, 2^16] (about +/-1.0) per component | Oracles.CyclicConvolutionComplexRaw — the O(N^2) definition-form sum destination[k] = sum over i of left[i] * right[(k - i) mod N], formed EXACTLY in BigInteger over the raw Q16 components at Q32 and rounded ONCE per component back to Q16 through the module's own RoundDyadic. The subject runs forward-forward-pointwise-inverse; the oracle never forwards, never inverts and never multiplies pointwise — the two share the convolution theorem and nothing else. Agreement within 64 raw Q16 ULPs per component — MEASURED: a calibration run at this envelope observed a worst case of 36 ULPs at length 256; 64 is that measurement with margin. | — | — |
| fft.convolution-vs-oracle-bound | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE: the bound is stated AT this amplitude and length range. The convolution's output grows as N times the product of the operands' amplitudes, and every twiddle's quantization error rides through three transforms and a pointwise product, so a caller at a wider envelope should expect proportionally larger absolute error. Unlike ntt.convolution-vs-oracle, agreement is a bound rather than exact equality: the fixed-point route rounds where the field route does not. | — | — | — |
| fft.convolution-vs-oracle-bound-deep | law: Deep | classical | — | MIRROR of fft.convolution-vs-oracle-bound at strictly stronger operands — lengths 512 through 4096 — with a wider measured bound (384 ULPs; the calibration run's worst case at this length range was 255 ULPs at length 4096), because three deeper transforms accumulate more per-stage rounding into an output that has itself grown with N | the same Oracles.CyclicConvolutionComplexRaw definition-form sum, at O(N^2) BigInteger cost up to N = 4096 | — | — |
| fft.impulse-dc-nyquist-exact | law: Default | structural | — | an impulse's spectrum is EXACTLY One at every bin, a constant (DC) input's spectrum is EXACTLY length*value at bin zero and EXACTLY zero at every other bin, and an alternating +/-value (Nyquist) input's spectrum is EXACTLY length*value at the top bin and EXACTLY zero elsewhere, at lengths 2 through 256. | — | — | — |
| fft.impulse-dc-nyquist-exact | law: Default | structural | — | these three are exact rather than bounded because every twiddle they touch is exactly +/-1 or +/-i, at which FixedComplex.operator* takes a leaf-product path whose two products are (value, 0) or (0, value) and whose sum-then-round therefore rounds NOTHING: the one-rounding kernel's rounding is a no-op on an already-exact input. A general bin (fft.round-trip-bound, fft.linearity-bound, fft.parseval-bound) touches a twiddle that is neither, so those are measured bounds instead. | — | — | — |
| fft.length-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | every documented refusal, asserted by exception TYPE and by the parameter name it reports: FixedFourierTransformPlan.Create at zero, a negative length and a non-power-of-two length (5); Forward and Inverse given a span whose length does not equal the plan's; ForwardReal given a real or destination span of the wrong length; InverseReal given a spectrum or destination span of the wrong length; Convolve given a left, right or destination span whose length does not equal the plan's; PointwiseMultiply given a right span or a destination span whose length differs from left, each naming its own parameter. | — | — | — |
| fft.linearity-bound | law: Default | structural | — | Forward(a) + Forward(b) agrees with Forward(a + b) within 24 raw Q16 ULPs per component, at lengths 1 through 256, over the same seeded envelope as fft.round-trip-bound. MEASURED: the calibration run's worst case at this length range was 13 ULPs at length 256; 24 is that measurement with margin. Unlike ntt.linearity-exact, the fixed-point transform's twiddle multiplies round independently on the a, b and a+b runs, so the two sides need not agree bit-for-bit even though the ideal (unrounded) DFT is exactly linear. | — | — | — |
| fft.linearity-bound-deep | law: Deep | structural | — | MIRROR of fft.linearity-bound at strictly stronger operands — lengths 512 through 4096 — with a wider measured bound (96 ULPs; the calibration run's worst case at this length range was 62 ULPs at length 4096). | — | — | — |
| fft.parseval-bound | law: Default | structural | — | sum(\|x_n\|^2) * length agrees with sum(\|X_k\|^2) — Parseval's identity for Forward's unscaled convention — within 4*10^11 raw Q32 units, at lengths 1 through 256 over the seeded envelope. Both sides are computed EXACTLY in BigInteger from the integer raw components (a raw squared is an exact integer, and their sum is exact), so the bound is on the fixed-point transform's own rounding and nothing else — no floating point enters the comparison at any point. MEASURED: the calibration run's worst case at this length range was about 2.6*10^11 at length 256. | — | — | — |
| fft.parseval-bound-deep | law: Deep | structural | — | MIRROR of fft.parseval-bound at strictly stronger operands — lengths 512 through 4096 — with a wider measured bound (6*10^13 raw Q32 units; the calibration run's worst case at this length range was about 4.0*10^13 at length 4096). | — | — | — |

A shifted overlap is refused before writing, by exception type and destination parameter name. A wiring statement about the lane loop rather than an accuracy statement about the product (complex.* pins that kernel): a lane skipped, an index crossed between the operands, or an aliasing read-after-write reddens this case. | — | — | — |
| fft.radix2-vs-direct-sum | law: Default | shared-substrate | fused-substrate | FixedFourierTransform.Forward's radix-2 decimation-in-time butterfly network, at lengths 1 through 32 | a direct O(N^2) DFT sum built in this claim body from the SAME FixedComplex.FromAngle and FixedComplex.operator* kernels Forward's twiddle table and butterflies use, but with a completely different summation schedule: no bit-reversal permutation, no stage decomposition, one running FixedComplex accumulator per output bin over all N terms rather than log2(N) pairwise combines. What this leg adds beyond those is the radix-2 SCHEDULE — the bit-reversal permutation and the stage-by-stage twiddle-stride indexing — which neither of those families touches: a swapped bit-reversal pair, a wrong twiddle stride, or a stage boundary off by one reddens this case while leaving scalar.* and complex.* green. |

| fft.round-trip-bound | law: Default | structural | — | Inverse(Forward(x)) recovers x within 64 raw Q16 ULPs per component, at lengths 1 through 256, over Pcg32XshRr-seeded operands in raw [-2^20, 2^20] (about +/-16.0). The bound is MEASURED: an independent calibration run at this exact envelope, seed source and length set observed a worst case of 39 ULPs at length 128; 64 is that measurement with margin, not a value chosen to make the case pass. | — | — | — |

Round-trip error scales with operand magnitude — each twiddle's own ~0.5 ULP quantization error (from FixedQ4816.SinCos) multiplies through the signal at every stage, so a caller working at a larger amplitude should expect proportionally larger absolute error, not this same ceiling. Forward's own XML doc states the argument. | — | — | — |

Rule 4's determinism contract: same input, same code version, bit-identical output on every run — this is the same-process purity half of that promise; it observes hidden mutable state or an operand-independent result and nothing else, and is never a pinned historical value (a correction to the kernel is expected to move the ACTUAL bits, never the fact that two runs agree with each other). | — | — | — |

| integer.hilbert-curve-refuses-outside-its-domain | law: Default | structural | — | every argument outside the documented domain is REFUSED rather than aliased onto one inside it: an order below one or past thirty-one, a coordinate at or past 2^order, a distance at or past 4^order. A bijective spatial key that maps distinct inputs together absorbs the caller's corruption instead of surfacing it | — | — | — |

| integer.ray-cycle-factors-are-not-writable-by-consumers | law: Default | structural | — | no public member of SymmetryLattice returns a collection a published marshal can unwrap into the process-wide backing array; a consumer's write to the value it IS handed does not survive to the next read; and the index bound refuses at both ends while staying reachable at the last position. Made by ATTEMPTING the escape rather than by reading a declared type, which is the error that let the first repair look complete: read-only is not ownership and neither is immutable. A ReadOnlyMemory yields its backing array to MemoryMarshal.TryGetArray and an ImmutableArray yields the same array to ImmutableCollectionsMarshal.AsArray -- both public, neither needing reflection or unsafe code, and either one let a consumer zero verified lattice metadata for every later consumer in the process. Count-and-index returning a value type by copy is the only shape with no route back | — | — | — |

| mass-properties.capsule-degenerates-to-sphere | law: Default | structural | — | THE DEGENERACY THAT PROVES THE CAPSULE'S OWN COEFFICIENTS. At a hemisphere-centre distance of zero a capsule IS a sphere, so TryCapsuleBody's mass and BOTH its moments must equal TrySphereBody's raws EXACTLY — not within a tolerance, because the two exact rationals coincide identically before either is rounded (the capsule's axial numerator collapses to 16/30 = 8/15 and its perpendicular numerator to 384/720 = 8/15, which is the sphere's own (8/15)*rho*pi*r^5). The identity that makes them coincide, 83/320 + (3/8)^2 = 2/5, is asserted FIRST as exact integers ((83*64 + 9*320)*5 == 2*(320*64)), so a failure says which half broke: the algebra or the kernel. A wrong 83/320 or a wrong 3r/8 offset would leave the perpendicular moment off while the axial one still matched, which is why both are compared. Swept over a bounded 4x4x3x3 ladder of densities, radii, length scales and result scales — a fixed step count, no search | — | — | — |
| mass-properties.capsule-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | FixedMassProperties.TryCapsuleBody — the mass and both moments of a solid capsule about its centre, stated with the hemisphere's own centroidal coefficient 83/320 and the parallel-axis offset (h/2 + 3r/8) | Oracles.TryCapsuleBody, THE independent derivation of this family: it assembles the capsule from its parts and never names 83/320 at all. A hemisphere's moment about the centre of its own FLAT FACE is (2/5)*m*r^2 — half a sphere's mass carrying half its moment about the same diameter — and its centroid sits 3r/8 from that face, so the parallel-axis theorem gives the centroidal moment as (2/5)m r^2 - m(3r/8)^2 and a SECOND transfer carries it out to the capsule's centre, a distance h/2 + 3r/8 away. Agreement is what proves the 83/320 coefficient, which appears on only one side | — | — |

| mass-properties.compound-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | FixedMassProperties.TryCompound (internal) — the summed mass, the composite centre of mass and the inertia tensor about that centre, for two swept parts; every part's parallel-axis contribution is taken against the EXACT rational centre rather than against the rounded centre the kernel reports | Oracles.TryCompound, which accumulates in the OPPOSITE order: every part's tensor is carried OUT to the shared origin, the parts are summed there, and the total is carried back IN to the composite centre by one reverse transfer. The subject transfers each part directly to the centre. The two routes are algebraically equal and computationally disjoint — they agree only if the transfer, the centre and both scale bridges are all right | — | — |

ENVELOPE: two parts, not an arbitrary count — the accumulation is a fold, so a third part exercises no branch the second does not, and the domain's lane budget is spent on the parts' own entries instead | — | — | — |
