All three tables are transcribed from the literature and derived nowhere in this repository |
| prime-field.baillie-psw-exhaustive | law: Exhaustive | structural | — | the composition's THESIS, checked instead of asserted: the two enumerated populations are DISJOINT. Beside it the sole-rejecter controls, which are what make both halves demonstrably load-bearing rather than decorative — the base-two round accepts every value on the Lucas list and the Lucas half accepts every value on the base-two list, so each half is the only thing rejecting the other half's pseudoprimes. On any sampled stream the two halves agree at every candidate, which is exactly the Baillie-PSW guarantee, so the conjunction is decidable ONLY at these populations | — | — | — |
| prime-field.baillie-psw-exhaustive | law: Exhaustive | structural | — | the degenerate shapes: 2,999 small perfect squares and eight squares of large primes are rejected, where no small factor screens the value out and the Selfridge search would otherwise run to its least prime factor; the d = 1 and s = 1 ladders at every width from 2^2 to 2^64, where one end puts the whole test in the squaring loop and the other never enters it; and every Fibonacci and Lucas term the carrier holds with its two neighbours on each side — the world the D = 5 parameter generates, which is the Lucas test's own worst case | — | — | — |
| prime-field.baillie-psw-exhaustive | law: Exhaustive | structural | — | ENVELOPE. This law is the gate of record for SCALE; prime-field.baillie-composition, prime-field.strong-round-vs-oracle and prime-field.lucas-vs-companion-matrix remain the gates of record for the statements at Default. Measured cost: about five minutes on six cores, dominated by the 2^32 sweep, which is why the whole law sits at Exhaustive. What it does NOT reach: the WITNESS BASE inside the composition is still unpinned — swapping the base two for the base three moves no answer below 10^7, and a value below 2^64 that moved one would itself be a Baillie-PSW counterexample of the class Feitsma and Galway rule out. The ladder at s = 64 is also unreached, because ulong.MaxValue fails the base-two round and the composition short-circuits before the Lucas half | — | — | — |
| prime-field.create-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | MaximumModulus is exactly 2^62, and Create REFUSES it and every value above it with an ArgumentOutOfRangeException naming the 'modulus' parameter — at the ceiling itself, one above it, and both carrier extremes. The bound is a REPRESENTATION invariant rather than a policy: it is what keeps Add and Subtract a single conditional fold, because two representatives then sum below 2^63 and never overflow the carrier | — | — | — |
| prime-field.create-and-refusals | law: Default | classical | — | every rung of the committed fifteen-rung modulus ladder, BEFORE Create is ever handed it | Oracles.ExactPrimality — trial division by the primes below 8192 and then twenty BigInteger strong-probable-prime rounds. No ladder constant is taken on its word, which is the same distrust binary-field.product-and-reduction-vs-oracle shows its own five moduli; a mistyped rung fails HERE, by name, rather than silently weakening every other case that runs the ladder. Both sides EXACT, so the substrate condition does not arise. ENVELOPE, and it is not the same statement at both ends of the ladder: the six rungs at or below 8191² = 67092481 are decided by TRIAL DIVISION, which shares no idea with anything in Puck.Maths, while the nine above it are decided by the twenty BigInteger rounds — whose base set opens with two, the base PrimeField64's own twelve-base IsPrime and its Baillie composition both run. Those nine rungs therefore share the CRITERION with the type they gate and differ in arithmetic, in base set and in loop structure only | — | — |
| prime-field.create-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | Create ACCEPTS every ladder rung the oracle proved prime, and the field it returns reports that modulus back, answers One as 1 and Zero as 0, equals a second field built over the same modulus — the record's whole value being its modulus — and PRINTS as exactly that one datum: ToString emits the modulus alone, the guarded identities kept out of the rendering by a hand-written PrintMembers because they are constants of the type rather than carried state | — | — | — |
| prime-field.create-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | an EVEN modulus is REFUSED with an ArgumentException naming 'modulus' at zero, two, four, six, 65536 and the largest even value below the ceiling. TWO is the historical corner and the reason the ladder carries it: the guard read `2 == (modulus & 1)`, a comparison a one-bit mask can never satisfy, so Create(2) was reachable and TrySqrt's non-residue walk never returned there | — | — | — |
| prime-field.create-and-refusals | law: Default | classical | — | Create's composite refusal over an odd-composite ladder — 1, 9, 15, 25, 561, and FOUR OF the psi_k strong pseudoprimes: the ones that force bases four, six, eight and eleven | Oracles.ExactPrimality, which independently classifies every one of them composite BEFORE the refusal is demanded. The psi rows are the discriminating ones: a modulus admitted on a short witness set would be a COMPOSITE modulus in a type whose whole contract is that the quotient ring is a field. ENVELOPE, twofold. EIGHT distinct psi values fit below the 2^62 ceiling rather than four; the other four force bases one, two, three and five and are exercised against IsPrime by prime-field.is-prime-vs-sieve-and-witness-ladder, not against Create's gate here. And the oracle is shared-nothing only over the low rows: 1, 9, 15, 25 and 561 are settled by TRIAL DIVISION, while all four psi rows sit above 8191² = 67092481 and are settled by twenty BigInteger rounds whose base set opens with the base-two round PrimeField64's own witness ladder runs — so those rows share the criterion and differ in arithmetic, base set and loop only | — | — |
| prime-field.create-and-refusals | law: Default | structural | — | a DEFAULT-INITIALIZED PrimeField64 is reachable — the record struct's private constructor does not stop `default(PrimeField64)`, and neither does an unassigned array element, which this case reaches through as well — and it REFUSES its whole semantic surface with InvalidOperationException: One, Zero, Add, Subtract, Negate, Multiply, Inverse, LegendreCharacter, Pow, both Reduce overloads, TrySqrt, and BatchInverse at length zero and length three. Each row is named in the failure text, so a member that quietly answers is reported as itself. The EMPTY batch is the row with teeth: the descriptor is read before the span is, so the zero-length early return cannot let an uninitialized field through unremarked. Modulus is deliberately OUTSIDE the policy and still reads zero, which is what keeps a default value printable and comparable — the array row asserts that equality still holds against `default`, and PRINTABILITY is asserted on ToString itself: a hand-written PrintMembers prints the modulus alone, so a default value formats as `PrimeField64 { Modulus = 0 }` instead of throwing from the guarded identities the compiler-synthesized member walk would have read. This statement REPLACES the earlier pin, under which Add, Subtract and Negate returned unreduced integer arithmetic with no diagnostic while Multiply, Reduce and Pow happened to raise DivideByZeroException from the zero modulus; that split was the defect rather than the contract, and the type now follows the house pattern FixedRateAccumulator sets | — | — | — |
| prime-field.inverse-and-batch | law: Default | classical | — | PrimeField64.Inverse and BatchInverse over a length ladder of 0, 1, 2, 3, 511, 512, 513 and 1024 elements — the ladder that straddles BatchInverse's 512-element stackalloc/ArrayPool boundary in BOTH directions | BigInteger.ModPow at exponent p − 2, computed per element and inline in Subjects.PrimeFieldInverseAndBatch. Both sides EXACT, so condition (B) drops out. The routes differ where it matters: the subject's batch accumulates a running product, inverts ONCE, and peels each element back off that single inverse in a backward pass, so an element's answer depends on every OTHER element in the region — a coupling the per-element oracle has no way to reproduce and a transposed prefix index would break immediately. ENVELOPE, because the two arms are NOT the same statement: for the SCALAR Inverse the reference shares the derivation. PrimeField64.Inverse is Pow(value, Modulus − 2) (PrimeField64.cs:382-386) and the reference is BigInteger.ModPow at that same exponent — Fermat against Fermat, differing in REPRESENTATION (Montgomery form against plain residues) and not in theorem, on an exponent prime-field.pow-vs-modpow already sweeps. What the scalar arm adds over that case is the delegation and the zero guard; the independent content of THIS case is the batch's running-product coupling | — | — |
| prime-field.inverse-and-batch | law: Default | structural | — | the scalar and the batch agree element for element at every ladder length, and every returned value multiplies with its input to One — so the batch is pinned twice over, against the oracle and against its own scalar sibling | — | — | — |
| prime-field.inverse-and-batch | law: Default | structural | — | zero has no inverse anywhere: Inverse REFUSES it with a DivideByZeroException, and BatchInverse refuses a region containing one at the first, a middle and the last index, because the shared running product is then zero | — | — | — |
| prime-field.inverse-and-batch | law: Default | structural | — | a REFUSED batch leaves the region bit-for-bit untouched. That is not decoration: the forward pass writes only its own scratch and the throw lands before the backward pass writes anything, so the failure is atomic — and the pooled scratch is returned in a finally on that path too | — | — | — |
| prime-field.inverse-and-batch | law: Default | structural | — | an EMPTY region is a no-op rather than a refusal, which is the early return the method opens with and the one length at which no scratch is taken at all | — | — | — |
| prime-field.inverse-and-batch | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE: the 1024-element rung runs at the 2^62 − 57 modulus only, and the short ladder at the remaining rungs. What that buys is the POOLED path exercised once at the widest arithmetic the type admits rather than four times over; the stack path is exercised at every rung. deep.prime-field-inverse-and-batch runs the long ladder at every rung instead. The rented array is longer than the request, and nothing here reads past the requested count | — | — | — |
| prime-field.inverse-and-batch | law: Default | structural | — | the POOLED scratch is CLEARED before it re-enters the shared pool: after a 1024-element batch, an immediate same-thread rent of the same bucket — the request ArrayPool.Shared serves from its thread-local slot, so an uncleared return would hand the very same array straight back — no longer carries the batch's first three hand-derived running products a0, a0·a1, a0·a1·a2. The kernel is the shared BatchInverseKernel, so the one clear covers QuadraticExtensionField64.BatchInverse and every future ring the kernel serves | — | — | — |
| prime-field.is-prime-vs-sieve-and-witness-ladder | law: Default | classical | — | PrimeField64.IsPrime at EVERY value through 20,000 — even, odd, zero and one included | Oracles.PrimeSieve, an ordinary sieve of Eratosthenes. This is the family's strongest anchor and the reason it comes first: the sieve carries no notion of a witness, a base, an exponent or a Montgomery form, so it shares with the subject not merely no code but no IDEA. Both sides EXACT, so condition (B) drops out. It is exhaustive over its band rather than sampled, so nothing in that band is a matter of luck | — | — |
| prime-field.is-prime-vs-sieve-and-witness-ladder | law: Default | classical | — | the twelve-base witness set, pinned base by base | Subjects.PrimeFieldWitnessPseudoprimes — eight (value, leading-base-count) rows drawn from the published psi_k table | — | psi_k is the LEAST composite that is a strong probable prime to the first k prime bases. The chain matters, because it is the LEAST-ness that this leg's counting rests on and it is not all one author's: Jaeschke (1993) determined psi_1 through psi_8 exactly and gave psi_9, psi_10 and psi_11 ≤ 3825123056546413051 as a BOUND, which later work proved least; Sorenson and Webster (2015) settled psi_12 = 318665857834031151167461 and psi_13. Each row's base count is DERIVED from that table rather than captured from any implementation: a value strictly below psi_(k+1) survives at most k leading bases, and psi_7 == psi_8 and psi_9 == psi_10 == psi_11 are why two rows read 8 and 11 rather than the indices the values are tabulated under. Every count is then MEASURED in the law by Oracles.ModularStrongProbablePrime, so a mistranscribed row fails rather than passing quietly |
| prime-field.is-prime-vs-sieve-and-witness-ladder | law: Default | structural | — | each pseudoprime row makes ONE FURTHER BASE load-bearing: truncating the twelve-base set to the row's count would accept that value as prime. That matters beyond this member: truncating the set from twelve bases to ELEVEN once went entirely undetected, passing every check then in place, including a 164,000-value replay above 10^12. Read that as history of what a large sampled sweep failed to catch — the replay itself is gone and does not stand behind this law — which is why the rows below carry their counts explicitly rather than trusting scale. ENVELOPE, re-spelled because the earlier wording over-claimed: the rows do NOT cover every truncation from one through eleven. They carry the counts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 11, and the published table contains no value whose leading-base count is exactly seven, nine or ten — a consequence of psi_7 == psi_8 and psi_9 == psi_10 == psi_11, which is a statement about the LEAST such composites and not a theorem about every value below 2^64. So bases eight, ten and eleven are pinned only JOINTLY with the neighbours they are truncated alongside, and this law does not reach them individually | — | — | — |
| prime-field.is-prime-vs-sieve-and-witness-ladder | law: Default | classical | — | IsPrime over a twenty-five-value carrier ladder — both sides of 2^31, 2^32, 2^61, 2^62 and 2^63, the largest prime below 2^32, the three values at the top of the carrier, and the smallest values where the guards outnumber the arithmetic | Oracles.ExactPrimality. ENVELOPE, stated rather than implied: through 8191² = 67092481 — just under 2^26 — that oracle decides by TRIAL DIVISION alone and shares no idea with the subject; above that band it runs twenty BigInteger strong-probable-prime rounds and so shares the CRITERION, differing in arithmetic (plain residues versus one shared ScaledResidueRing64), in base set (twenty is a strict superset of twelve) and in loop structure. That upper leg therefore pins the subject's arithmetic, its witness loop, its Montgomery encoding and its witness set — and does not independently re-derive the completeness theorem, which is a third-party computation on both sides | — | — |
| prime-field.is-prime-vs-witness-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | PrimeField64.IsPrime over the swept candidate stream — both drawn raws read as ulong and each additionally forced odd, so the sweep meets the arithmetic and not only the even short-circuit — across the WHOLE carrier, which is where the sieve band cannot reach | Oracles.ExactPrimality. Both sides EXACT, so condition (B) drops out. ENVELOPE, the same one prime-field.is-prime-vs-sieve-and-witness-ladder's ladder leg states and stated again because this law lives almost entirely above it: through 8191² the oracle is trial division and shares no idea with the subject; above it the oracle runs twenty BigInteger rounds against the subject's twelve Montgomery ones, so the criterion is shared and the arithmetic, the base set and the loop are not | — | — |
| prime-field.is-prime-vs-witness-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the edge battery is what makes this sweep bite rather than merely run: read as ulong, the committed edge set carries 0, 1, 2^64 − 1, 2^63, 2^63 ± 1, 2^31 ± 1, 2^47 ± 1 and the two's-complement images of every negative raw, so the carrier's corners — where the odd-part split, the trailing-zero count and the ring's radix reduction are all at their extremes — are swept on every run rather than sampled | — | — | — |
| prime-field.is-prime-vs-witness-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | MIRROR-ADJACENT, and named so no reader over-reads it: this law SAMPLES where prime-field.montgomery-chains-exhaustive sweeps EVERY value from zero through 10^6 against a sieve of Eratosthenes and the whole contiguous 100,000-value band at 9·10^11 against a segmented one. That law is the gate of record for SCALE, at the Exhaustive tier; this law is the gate of record for the statement, at Default | — | — | — |
| prime-field.legendre-vs-reciprocity | law: Default | classical | — | PrimeField64.LegendreCharacter at five ladder rungs on the folded swept operand — Euler's exponentiation criterion, one Montgomery chain per call | Oracles.JacobiSymbolReciprocity — the binary quadratic-reciprocity descent in BigInteger, which at a PRIME modulus is the Legendre symbol. A genuinely different derivation route rather than a re-spelling: the subject raises to (p − 1)/2 and reads the answer off a power, the oracle never exponentiates at all. Both sides EXACT, so condition (B) drops out. The oracle calls NO Puck.Maths member — in particular it is not NumberTheoryFunctions.JacobiSymbol, which is a SUBJECT of core.jacobi-symbol-cross-carrier, nor UnsignedNumberFunctions.JacobiSymbol, which IsStrongLucasProbablePrime itself calls | — | — |
| prime-field.legendre-vs-reciprocity | law: Default | classical | — | the same character, a second time | BigInteger.ModPow at exponent (p − 1)/2, inline in the same claim body — the THIRD route, and the one that anchors the reciprocity descent itself rather than merely the subject. Two references that share nothing with each other and nothing with the subject must both agree, so a defect in the new oracle cannot pass as agreement | — | — |
| prime-field.legendre-vs-reciprocity | law: Default | structural | — | the character is MULTIPLICATIVE on the swept pair — the character of a product is the product of the characters, zeros included — and a square always reports +1. Neither statement can be satisfied by a reciprocity descent that lost its sign or by an exponentiation that lost its bit | — | — | — |
| prime-field.legendre-vs-reciprocity | law: Default | structural | — | the character is exactly zero at zero and never at any other reduced element, which is the one branch LegendreCharacter takes before it exponentiates at all | — | — | — |
| prime-field.legendre-vs-reciprocity | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE: the law folds every operand into [0, p) before it asks. LegendreCharacter does NOT enforce its reduced-operand precondition, and an unreduced argument reaches Encode, which folds it — so an unreduced multiple of p would be reported as a non-square rather than as zero. That regime is outside this statement by construction. It cannot leak through the extension factory: extension-field.construction-and-refusals proves Create rejects the modulus and other unreduced generators BEFORE consulting the character, which is the validating boundary responsible for enforcing LegendreCharacter's hot-path precondition | — | — | — |
| prime-field.lucas-vs-companion-matrix | law: Default | classical | — | PrimeField64.IsStrongLucasProbablePrime over the swept candidate stream, forced odd, across the WHOLE carrier | Oracles.StrongLucasSelfridge — the same test computed from 2×2 COMPANION-MATRIX powers in BigInteger. Both sides EXACT, so condition (B) drops out. Three deliberate divergences make this independent rather than a re-spelling: the subject walks the U/V doubling identities most-significant-bit first with HALVINGS on every index-incrementing step, entirely inside ScaledResidueRing64, while the oracle multiplies matrices in plain residues, halves nothing anywhere, and carries no V recurrence at all — it derives V_d from two consecutive U terms. A wrong index-incrementing pair, a dropped Q^k squaring, or a halving that leaves the carrier shows here and nowhere else. It is also O(log n), so this leg reaches the whole carrier where an index-by-index recurrence oracle would stop in the tens of thousands | — | — |
| prime-field.lucas-vs-companion-matrix | law: Default | classical | — | the Selfridge Method A parameter search — the discriminant the whole test is defined by | the same search inside Oracles.StrongLucasSelfridge, walking SIGNED BigInteger candidates with the sign carried explicitly (the subject reads it off `magnitude & 3`) and taking its symbol from Oracles.JacobiSymbolReciprocity, this suite's own reciprocity descent. This CLOSES the OWED that stands over any Lucas oracle taking its symbol from NumberTheoryFunctions.JacobiSymbol, the BigInteger sibling of the very function the subject's search calls: a wrong symbol would pick the same discriminant on both sides. Here it cannot: the two symbols are separate implementations with no shared line. This leg is also what licenses the UnsignedNumberFunctions.JacobiSymbol citation on this case: the subject's search reads that member's SIGN at every swept candidate, and inverting the returned sign reddens this law together with prime-field.baillie-composition and prime-field.pseudoprime-populations. What the citation claims is the sign and nothing wider — the cross-carrier agreement and the composite-modulus regime are core.jacobi-symbol-cross-carrier, where the composite regime stands against the symbol's factor-and-Euler DEFINITION rather than against the library's own sibling descent, and the class this law cannot reach is the ENVELOPE below | — | — |
| prime-field.lucas-vs-companion-matrix | law: Default | structural | — | the direction the test decides outright: EVERY PRIME PASSES. The candidate's primality is settled independently by Oracles.ExactPrimality, and where it is prime the test is required to accept — a false reject that no differential against another probable-prime test could see | — | — | — |
| prime-field.lucas-vs-companion-matrix | law: Default | structural | — | perfect squares are rejected, at the adversarial shape: the square of a large value, where no small factor screens it out and the parameter search would otherwise run to the value's least prime factor. The oracle decides squareness by BISECTION on the root — exact, float-free, thirty-two halvings — deliberately NOT by the subject's own ulong.SquareRoot, whose first estimate comes from hardware floating point and is the single floating-point touch the whole wing admits to. A gate must not read the estimate it gates | — | — | — |
| prime-field.lucas-vs-companion-matrix | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE: the Selfridge search is UNBOUNDED — no step budget, and its ulong magnitude counter can wrap. Its termination rests on a theorem rather than on a validation, so a defect that suppressed the −1 outcome would hang or wrap rather than redden this law; wrapped, the sign is read off `magnitude & 3`, which is meaningless for an even magnitude. An unbounded search whose predicate is a subject owes two clauses with DISTINCT messages — a deterministic step budget, which names a broken predicate, and a wrap guard, which names an exhausted range — and the wrap half is not hypothetical: FirstPrimeAtOrAbove(2^64 − 40) returned 3, having stepped past the carrier and wrapped, a wrong ANSWER that no step budget can catch. The subject has neither clause, and no law can supply one from outside. Stated here because nothing in this suite can catch it. It is also the exact boundary of this case's UnsignedNumberFunctions.JacobiSymbol citation, and the campaign probed both sides of it: inverting the symbol's returned sign REDDENS this law, while perturbing the two-indicator shift so the −1 outcome is never produced HANGS the run instead | — | — | — |
| prime-field.lucas-vs-companion-matrix | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE: the perfect-square pre-check is a COST bound and not a termination guarantee — candidates step by two and so sweep every odd number, one of which shares a factor with the value, and the vanishing-symbol exit fires there anyway — so this law's square rows pin the ANSWER at squares and say nothing about why the search halts. Delete the guard and n = 25 still returns after one candidate and n = 9 after six; what it buys is COST, since without it a square spends Jacobi evaluations proportional to its least prime factor. Every check that appears to gate the guard passes identically with it removed, these square rows included | — | — | — |
| prime-field.montgomery-chains-exhaustive | law: Exhaustive | classical | — | PrimeField64.IsPrime at EVERY value from zero through 10^6, composite as well as prime | Oracles.PrimeSieve — a plain sieve of Eratosthenes: crossed-out multiples and surviving flags, sharing with the subject not merely no code but no IDEA. Both sides EXACT, so condition (B) drops out | — | — |
| prime-field.montgomery-chains-exhaustive | law: Exhaustive | classical | — | PrimeField64.IsPrime over the CONTIGUOUS 100,000-value band starting at 900,000,000,001 — an order of magnitude past where 32-bit primality reaches, and dense rather than sampled, because a verdict wrong for one residue class cannot hide in a contiguous sweep the way it can in a random one | a SEGMENTED sieve of Eratosthenes written in PrimalityScaleClaims.cs, crossing out the multiples of every prime below 10^6 across the window. It is exact only while the window stays under the square of the smallest prime the list OMITS, and that bound is read off the generated list at run time rather than restated as a literal beside it, so a widened window fails the guard instead of silently degrading the oracle | — | — |
| prime-field.montgomery-chains-exhaustive | law: Exhaustive | classical | — | PrimeField64.Pow, in Montgomery form, over thirty-two prime moduli spanning three to the 2^62 ceiling — the smallest odd primes, the widening multiply's 2^32 seam, and the ceiling from both sides — at twelve residues by eleven exponents each, the exponents including zero, one, both Fermat/Euler exponents and both carrier edges, plus 20,000 randomized full-width exponents so the chain length varies | BigInteger.ModPow. Both sides EXACT. The subject performs no hardware division and never leaves Montgomery form; the reference is plain arbitrary-width residues. Verifying Montgomery against Montgomery would prove nothing, which is why the substrate is probed only through the public surfaces it powers | — | — |
| prime-field.montgomery-chains-exhaustive | law: Exhaustive | classical | — | PrimeField64.Multiply, which deliberately stayed on the divide rather than joining the chain, and PrimeField64.Inverse and PrimeField64.BatchInverse, which ride it | the exact product (a·b) mod m in BigInteger for the one-shot multiply — its own oracle, not the chain's, because it is not on the chain — and BigInteger.ModPow at exponent modulus−2 for both inverses. BatchInverse turns thirty-seven elements over through one Inverse and is compared element by element, so a misplaced prefix product shows as a position rather than as a bulk mismatch | — | — |
| prime-field.montgomery-chains-exhaustive | law: Exhaustive | classical | — | PrimeField64.LegendreCharacter and the accept/reject decision of PrimeField64.TrySqrt, at every swept residue of every modulus on the ladder | Oracles.JacobiSymbolReciprocity — the binary quadratic-reciprocity descent in BigInteger, which never exponentiates at all, against Euler's criterion, which is nothing but exponentiation. Two derivations with no shared step. The reference is outside Puck.Maths entirely rather than the shipped fixed-width JacobiSymbol, which is what makes the leg classical rather than in-tree-independent | — | — |
| prime-field.montgomery-chains-exhaustive | law: Exhaustive | classical | — | PrimeField64.IsPrime across eight sampled bands straddling the widening seam, the 2^62 field ceiling and the top of the carrier, plus a dense 4,000-value run at the very top where every reduction rides the wrapping-quotient path, and the carrier's largest prime located by the subject under an explicit 800-step budget | Oracles.ExactPrimality — trial division by the primes below 8192, then TWENTY strong-probable-prime rounds evaluated entirely in BigInteger against a base set that is a strict SUPERSET of the subject's twelve Montgomery ones. ENVELOPE: above the trial-division band the criterion is shared and the arithmetic, the base set and the loop are not | — | — |
| prime-field.montgomery-chains-exhaustive | law: Exhaustive | classical | — | PrimeField64.IsPrime on the four tabulated psi_k values — 3215031751, 3474749660383, 341550071728321 and 3825123056546413051 — each of which is a strong probable prime to every one of the first k prime bases, so truncating the twelve-base witness set to k accepts it and NOTHING else in this suite notices | the tabulated psi_k table, each row carrying the measured number of leading bases the value actually survives rather than the index it is catalogued under: 341550071728321 is tabulated as psi_7 and survives eight, 3825123056546413051 is tabulated as psi_9 and survives eleven | — | the psi_k values are Sorenson and Webster's published least strong pseudoprimes to the first k prime bases, transcribed from the literature and derived nowhere in this repository; the surviving-base counts beside them were measured here against Oracles.ModularStrongProbablePrime |
| prime-field.montgomery-chains-exhaustive | law: Exhaustive | structural | — | the square-root contract, self-standing: every residue's SQUARE roots and the root squares back, a residue roots exactly when its character is not −1, and where it does the returned root squares to it. Beside them, 5,000 semiprimes constructed from two 32-bit primes are rejected — composite by construction, so no oracle is needed, and one-sided by nature: the probe can catch a false accept and can never catch a false reject | — | — | — |
| prime-field.montgomery-chains-exhaustive | law: Exhaustive | structural | — | ENVELOPE. This law is the gate of record for SCALE: prime-field.is-prime-vs-witness-oracle and prime-field.pow-vs-modpow remain the gates of record for the statements at Default, and this law is where the exhaustive 0..10^6 sweep and the contiguous 100,000-value band at 9·10^11 actually run. Measured cost on six cores: about one second, so the Exhaustive tier here buys scale rather than time. What it does NOT reach: the moduli are prime, so nothing here says anything about Create being handed a composite; and the 5,000 semiprimes top out near 4.4·10^18, below 2^62, so they do not exercise the widest reduction — the carrier-top run above owns that | — | — | — |
| prime-field.pow-vs-modpow | law: Default | classical | — | PrimeField64.Pow at five ladder rungs and five exponents per operand — the swept full-width exponent, zero, one, p − 2 and (p − 1)/2 — which is this family's HOT PATH: Inverse, LegendreCharacter, TrySqrt's descent and all four primality entry points reach their arithmetic through this one chain | BigInteger.ModPow, inline in Subjects.PrimeFieldPowMatchesModularPower. Both sides EXACT, so condition (B) drops out. The routes differ in REPRESENTATION, not merely in code: the subject converts into ScaledResidueRing64 once, runs square-and-multiply with a per-bit conditional multiply, and converts back once, so every intermediate is a Montgomery image; the oracle stays in plain residues from first to last. A representation leak — the second of this family's named failure modes — is exactly what disagreement here catches | — | — |
| prime-field.pow-vs-modpow | law: Default | structural | — | the exponent's two poles are exact rather than approximated: the zeroth power is One for EVERY base including zero, which is the documented convention, and the first power moves nothing | — | — | — |
| prime-field.pow-vs-modpow | law: Default | structural | — | Fermat's little theorem closes the chain at every rung: a^(p−1) is One for every non-zero a and zero for a = 0, a statement whose truth depends on the modulus really being prime and so on Create's own gate, which prime-field.create-and-refusals pins against the oracle | — | — | — |
| prime-field.pow-vs-modpow | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE: Pow's operation count depends on the exponent and the routine is deliberately NOT constant-time in it, so nothing here is a timing statement. What the five-exponent ladder buys is schedule breadth — a zero-bit exponent, a one-bit exponent, and two exponents whose expansions are dense across the whole width — not a claim about the shape of the chain | — | — | — |
| prime-field.pseudoprime-populations | law: Default | classical | — | the two pseudoprime POPULATIONS below 10^4, ENUMERATED by the subjects themselves rather than looked up — every odd composite in the band is offered to the base-two round and to the strong Lucas test | Oracles.PrimeSieve, an ordinary sieve of Eratosthenes, which decides which candidates are composite in the first place and so fixes the band the enumeration runs over. It carries no notion of a witness, a base or a Lucas parameter, so it shares with the subjects not merely no code but no idea. Both sides EXACT, so condition (B) drops out | — | — |
| prime-field.pseudoprime-populations | law: Default | classical | — | the two enumerated populations, compared list against list | Subjects.PrimeFieldBaseTwoPseudoprimes — 2047, 3277, 4033, 4681, 8321 — and Subjects.PrimeFieldLucasPseudoprimes — 5459, 5777 | — | OEIS A001262, the strong pseudoprimes to base 2, and OEIS A217255, the strong Lucas pseudoprimes for the Selfridge Method A parameters (Baillie and Wagstaff, 1980) — which is the parameter choice the subject runs, and without which the second list names nothing. Both rows are the below-10^4 prefixes of published sequences, so this is a property of the TESTS rather than a pin captured off the implementation. What the enumeration adds over a lookup is the other direction: it catches a test that GAINED a pseudoprime as well as one that lost a rejection, and the published list is what says which population is the right one |
| prime-field.pseudoprime-populations | law: Default | classical | — | the seven Carmichael numbers, rejected by the composition and by IsPrime | Subjects.PrimeFieldCarmichaelNumbers — 561, 1105, 1729, 2465, 2821, 6601, 8911 | — | the published Carmichael numbers — absolute pseudoprimes, composite yet Fermat probable prime to every coprime base — which is the weakness both halves of the composition are built to survive. Named honestly: all seven die at the base-two STRONG round, so as a probe of the Lucas half this row cannot fail; it gates the composition's Fermat-weakness claim and nothing else |
| prime-field.pseudoprime-populations | law: Default | structural | — | the composition's whole THESIS, checked instead of asserted: the two enumerated populations are DISJOINT. That is the only reason a conjunction of two probable-prime tests is worth more than either half | — | — | — |
| prime-field.pseudoprime-populations | law: Default | structural | — | the sole-rejecter controls, which make both halves demonstrably load-bearing rather than decorative: the base-two round ACCEPTS every strong Lucas pseudoprime, so the Lucas half is what rejects it; the Lucas test ACCEPTS every base-two strong pseudoprime, so the round is what rejects it; and the composition rejects both populations. This is probable-ness pinned as a FACT — these tests are REQUIRED to accept composites, and the law says so rather than apologising for it | — | — | — |
| prime-field.pseudoprime-populations | law: Default | structural | — | IsPrime rejects every value in both populations and every Carmichael number, which is what separates the exact decision from the two probable ones on exactly the values where they differ | — | — | — |
| prime-field.pseudoprime-populations | law: Default | structural | — | the smallest values, where the guards outnumber the arithmetic: 0, 1 and the small composites are rejected by both tests and by the composition; every prime below 100 is accepted by all three | — | — | — |
| prime-field.sqrt-descent-and-refusal | law: Default | classical | — | TrySqrt's ACCEPT/REJECT decision at five ladder rungs — a decision it makes for itself, before any root exists, by raising the operand to (p − 1)/2 inside the ring | Oracles.JacobiSymbolReciprocity: the operand is a square exactly when the reciprocity symbol is not −1. Both sides EXACT, so condition (B) drops out, and the routes could not be further apart — one exponentiates in Montgomery form, the other descends by reciprocity in BigInteger and never forms a power | — | — |
| prime-field.sqrt-descent-and-refusal | law: Default | structural | — | the root is checked by SQUARING IT BACK rather than against a reference root, which is the only honest statement available: a square has two roots and the method promises neither one in particular. Both roots are exercised — the returned r and its sibling Negate(r) = p − r — and both must square back to the operand; the two coincide only at zero | — | — | — |
| prime-field.sqrt-descent-and-refusal | law: Default | structural | — | a REFUSED TrySqrt returns false AND leaves zero in the out parameter, at every rung, so the failed call carries no stale value out | — | — | — |
| prime-field.sqrt-descent-and-refusal | law: Default | structural | — | zero roots to zero and returns true, the one operand that short-circuits ahead of the character decision entirely | — | — | — |
| prime-field.sqrt-descent-and-refusal | law: Default | structural | — | the character TrySqrt decides for itself agrees with LegendreCharacter on the SAME operand stream — the two cases share the domain key prime-field-root, so this is a statement about identical operands rather than about two sweeps that happen to overlap | — | — | — |
| prime-field.sqrt-descent-and-refusal | law: Default | structural | — | the ladder straddles BOTH of TrySqrt's arms, and the claim ASSERTS that rather than assuming it: rungs congruent to 3 modulo 4 take the direct power value^((p + 1)/4), rungs congruent to 1 modulo 4 take the nonresidue-assisted descent, and the body counts both and fails if the ladder ever stops carrying one. The 3·2^30 + 1 rung is the deep descent — a 2-adic valuation of 30 in p − 1, so the correction loop runs many rounds — and the 17 rung is its degenerate opposite, where the odd part of p − 1 is ONE | — | — | — |
| prime-field.sqrt-descent-and-refusal | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE: the descent's walk to the smallest non-residue is an UNBOUNDED search with no step budget and a ulong counter that could in principle wrap. Its termination rests on a theorem (non-residues are half the non-zero residues), not on a validation, so a defect that made the ring's minus-one unreachable would HANG rather than redden this law. A hang is not a red test. An unbounded search whose predicate is a subject owes two clauses with DISTINCT messages — a deterministic step budget, which names a broken predicate, and a wrap guard, which names an exhausted range. The subject has neither, and no law can supply one from outside — so the failure mode is named here because nothing in this suite can catch it | — | — | — |
| prime-field.strong-round-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | PrimeField64.IsStrongProbablePrime over the swept candidate stream at six witness bases per candidate — the swept full-width base, zero, one, two, value − 1 and value itself — on both the drawn value and its forced-odd image | Oracles.ModularStrongProbablePrime, one strong round evaluated entirely in BigInteger. Both sides EXACT, so condition (B) drops out. The routes differ in REPRESENTATION rather than in criterion, and that is the point: the subject never leaves Montgomery form, comparing its power against the ring's own encoded One and NegativeOne, where the oracle compares plain residues against 1 and value − 1. A representation leak is what disagreement catches; the criterion itself is shared and this leg does not claim otherwise | — | — |
| prime-field.strong-round-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the contract's own zero-base clause, which is the one clause a reader would not guess: a base that reduces to zero carries no evidence and PASSES. Both witness = 0 and witness = value are exercised at every ODD candidate above two, and the oracle carries the same clause, so the two AGREE about it rather than one of them merely implementing it. ENVELOPE, and it is where this clause actually lives: the clause sits BELOW the guards in subject and oracle alike, so an even candidate is rejected before its base is ever reduced and the zero base does not pass there — which the guard row below states directly rather than leaving as an apparent exception | — | — | — |
| prime-field.strong-round-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the direction a probable-prime test decides OUTRIGHT: every prime passes every base. The candidate's primality is settled independently by Oracles.ExactPrimality and, where it is prime, all six rounds are required to accept — so a false REJECT is caught here, which is the failure a differential against a probable-prime sibling can never see | — | — | — |
| prime-field.strong-round-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the guards below the arithmetic: values under two are rejected, two is accepted, and every even value above two is rejected, at every base | — | — | — |
| prime-field.strong-round-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE: a passed round proves nothing about primality and this law never says it does. What it pins is that the round is the round it CLAIMS to be. The composition's own thesis — that this round's pseudoprimes and the Lucas test's are disjoint populations — is pinned in prime-field.pseudoprime-populations, not here. This law and its two neighbours share the domain key prime-field-primality, so all three speak about one candidate stream | — | — | — |
| q1648.add-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | FixedQ1648.op_Addition | Oracles.WrapToRaw over an exact BigInteger sum — EXACT on both sides, so condition (B) drops out entirely and the statement is purely the two's-complement wrapping policy | — | — |
| q1648.additive-ops-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | FixedQ1648.op_Subtraction | Oracles.WrapToRaw over an exact BigInteger difference — EXACT on both sides, so condition (B) drops out and the statement is purely the two's-complement wrapping policy | — | — |
| q1648.additive-ops-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | FixedQ1648.op_UnaryNegation, op_Increment and op_Decrement | Oracles.WrapToRaw over the exact BigInteger −a, a + 2⁴⁸ and a − 2⁴⁸ — exact on both sides | — | — |
| q1648.additive-ops-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | unary plus is the identity at every swept raw, and negation is an involution over the full raw range including MinValue, where the two's-complement negation is its own fixed point | — | — | — |
| q1648.additive-ops-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | the increment and decrement operators are mutually inverse at every swept raw, and each equals the corresponding addition of One | — | — | — |
| q1648.checked-ops-refuse | law: Default | classical | — | all seven checked operators — addition, subtraction, unary negation, increment, decrement, multiplication and division — over every swept operand pair | the exact BigInteger value of each operation, which decides BOTH halves of the statement: the operator must return that value when it lands inside [−2⁶³, 2⁶³ − 1] and must throw OverflowException when it does not. The multiplication's expected value is a locally derived Q1648ExactRoundedProduct and the division's Q1648ExactRoundedRatio, both routing through the SAME shared Oracles.RoundRationalTiesToEven body FixedQ4816's own ExactRoundedProduct/ExactRoundedRatio use, at shift 48 rather than their hardcoded 16, both UNWRAPPED, so the checked contract is decided by the exact rounded value rather than by the unchecked sibling | — | — |
| q1648.checked-ops-refuse | law: Default | structural | — | the seven checked operators agree BIT-FOR-BIT with their unchecked siblings on every operand pair whose exact value is representable — a wrapping operator and its checked twin differ only in the refusal, never in the answer | — | — | — |
| q1648.checked-ops-refuse | law: Default | structural | — | the two documented division refusals are distinct and both reachable: a zero divisor throws DivideByZeroException from BOTH the checked and the unchecked operator, and MinValue over NegativeOne throws OverflowException from the checked operator while the unchecked one wraps to MinValue | — | — | — |
| q1648.decimal-conversion-modes | law: Default | classical | — | the three INumberBase conversion hooks (TryConvertFromChecked/Saturating/Truncating, reached only through T.CreateChecked/CreateSaturating/CreateTruncating<FixedQ1648, decimal> since they are explicit interface implementations) at decimal.MaxValue, decimal.MinValue, and an in-range decimal — the only route to FixedPointConvert.ScaleDecimalWide, which q1648.text-round-trip and scalar.generic-conversion-modes never reach (the latter is hardcoded to FixedQ4816/UFixedQ4816, both of which route decimal through the narrower ScaleDecimal instead) | the exact scaled value re-derived independently from decimal.GetBits and Oracles.RoundRationalTiesToEven at shift 48 — never through ScaleDecimalWide — including a hand-verified bit-layout derivation of decimal.MaxValue's own mantissa (2^96 - 1, scale 0) that the oracle is checked against before being trusted | — | — |
| q1648.divide-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | FixedQ1648.op_Division — the hardware 128-by-64 quotient under the raw_x >> 16 < raw_y gate, its UInt128 fallback, the r versus d − r tie test, and the magnitude-wrap-then-negate sign policy (structurally FixedQ4816.op_Division's shift-16-generalized sibling, at shift 48) | Oracles.RoundDyadicRatio at shift 48 — ONE ties-to-even rounding of the exact rational (raw_x·2⁴⁸)/raw_y in BigInteger, wrapped once at the end by Oracles.WrapToRaw. ENVELOPE: the synthetic span is evidence about the ORDER of the gates and nothing else — no element of it is ever dereferenced, and a build that removed the guard would fault rather than report | — | — | — |

| sampling.bit-mix-constants-invert | law: Default | structural | — | the two multiplier/inverse pairs multiply to ONE modulo 2^32, and both multipliers are odd — an algebraic fact about the declared constants that holds whether or not Mix is ever called, and the first thing a mistyped digit breaks. ENVELOPE: this pins the shifts as CORRECT for the inversion, not as GOOD for mixing — avalanche quality is not a correctness claim and no leg here makes one | — | — | — |

| sampling.bit-mix-is-a-permutation | law: Exhaustive | structural | — | Unmix(Mix(x)) == x at EVERY one of the 2^32 words, swept in 256 partitions across cores and reporting the smallest counterexample so the message is scheduling-independent. This is the net property restated in the terms the GPU sampler actually reads in, which nothing else in the suite exercises: the cone-table law pins the stored values' norm and distinctness and this file's other new laws pin the net property and the shuffle's aligned-block law separately, but none of them ties ShuffleIndex's output directly to the cone table's own declared entry counts the way a GPU consumer's draw sequence does | — | — | — |
| sampling.cone-table-build-purity-and-quantized-coverage | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE: no floating-point arithmetic enters this law. Re-deriving each polar entry's expected bits from Math.Tan and Math.Sqrt of the specific half-angle 0.11 and comparing bit for bit would put float arithmetic INSIDE the gate, which this suite's rules forbid in law logic, and sampling.cone-table-stored-norm-and-uniqueness's own leg already argues its exact-envelope check is the better statement ('a reader that silently measured the pre-rounding doubles the builder discarded ... would be reported rather than passed'). That double-rounded-value comparison is therefore deliberately absent here; it is superseded, not owed | — | — | — |
| sampling.cone-table-stored-norm-and-uniqueness | law: Default | structural | — | the stored-norm envelope, measured on what a CONSUMER reads back: for all 4096 azimuth pairs and all 4096 polar pairs, at each of six half-angles, \|stored² + stored² − 1\| ≤ 2⁻²³ + 2⁻⁴⁰. The bound is DERIVED FROM THE FORMAT and not recorded from a run — two independent binary32 roundings at a relative error of at most the 2⁻²⁴ unit roundoff move the squared norm by at most 2·2⁻²⁴, and the second term absorbs their product and the double-side construction's own rounding with room to spare. The measurement is EXACT: each component's square is an integer shift of a 24-bit integer square, and the whole comparison runs in BigInteger at a common scale of 2⁻⁴⁰⁰, so no float arithmetic enters the law that judges a float table | — | — | — |
| sampling.cone-table-stored-norm-and-uniqueness | law: Default | structural | — | the envelope BITES rather than decorating: the law asserts that the worst departure across the whole ladder is strictly positive, so a table that happened to store exactly unit pairs — or a reader that silently measured the pre-rounding doubles the builder discarded — would be reported rather than passed | — | — | — |
| sampling.cone-table-stored-norm-and-uniqueness | law: Default | structural | — | uniqueness as the contract now states it — a property of the half-angle rather than a promise made for all of them. At the zero half-angle all 4096 polar entries are the identical axis pair (1, 0), because a cap of zero angle IS one direction, and at each of 0.01, π/6, π/3 and the closest double below π/2 the 4096 cells resolve into 4096 distinct stored pairs, counted rather than sampled. The old XML said cell-centre sampling means quantization `never produces a duplicated or degenerate direction`, unconditionally, while the same member's parameter documentation admitted the zero cap that duplicates every entry; the XML and src/Puck.Maths/Sampling/README.md are both re-spelled in this change, so the law and the prose state one thing. ENVELOPE: distinctness is asserted at those four rungs and is NOT claimed for every positive half-angle — as the angle shrinks the entries approach the axis and coincide there below binary32's resolution, continuously, exactly as the geometry does | — | — | — |
| sampling.cone-table-stored-norm-and-uniqueness | law: Default | structural | — | the ±0.0 policy, decided in this change rather than inherited: a negative-zero half-angle is admitted and is NOT canonicalized. It stores radial bits 0x80000000 where +0.0 stores 0x00000000, and the axial word is 0x3F800000 either way, so the two tables differ in exactly the sign of a zero — unobservable, because a zero radial scales the whole azimuth contribution away. Both bit patterns are asserted by value, so the policy cannot drift into whichever the runtime happened to produce, and both the XML and the wing README now state it | — | — | — |
| sampling.cone-table-stored-norm-and-uniqueness | law: Default | structural | — | the layout, read into locals before comparison so the run makes the comparison rather than the compiler folding it away — TableIndexBitCount 12, both entry counts 2¹², DirectionNumberOffset zero, AzimuthOffset the plane's direction-number count, and each further offset the previous plus twice its table — and the direction-number prefix compared word for word against DigitalNetSampler.BuildPlaneDirectionNumbers at every rung, so the builder's own opening slice is pinned rather than assumed | — | — | — |

What this case states is exactly what survives that: the storage rounding, the layout, the refusals, and the uniqueness policy — every one of them a statement about the FORMAT rather than about the platform's transcendental library | — | — | — |

| sampling.digital-net-shifted-and-shuffled-blocks-are-nets | law: Default | structural | — | the (0, m, 2)-net property survives EACH of 64 pseudorandom digital shifts -- drawn from Pcg32XshRr.Create(state: 0x5EED, stream: 0x11) and fed through DeriveScramble exactly as a consumer would derive one -- at every order 1 through 12. This closes the gap sampling.digital-net-identities-and-net-property's own leg names: 'the digital shift's box-preservation is asserted here only at the one shift vector'. The underlying theorem (a digital shift is an affine bijection of the coordinate's bits, so it carries dyadic boxes onto dyadic boxes of the same shape) is stated in DigitalNetSampler's own remarks and is true for every shift vector, but an implementation defect tied to a PARTICULAR scramble bit pattern -- for example in FillPoints or the scramble derivation -- is exactly what one fixed shift cannot catch and 64 independently drawn ones can. MIRROR of that leg at a materially wider shift population -- 64 drawn shifts rather than one -- at the same order-12 depth | — | — | — |

This is a DIFFERENT structural fact from the aligned-block law sampling.digital-net-identities-and-net-property already proves (that the block LANDS somewhere aligned) and from this file's sibling law (that the IDENTITY block is a net) -- it is the composition DigitalNetSampler's own remarks assert and that no existing law exercises end to end: 'every such block of a (0, 2)-sequence is itself a (0, m, 2)-net, so a consumer's own first 2^m draws are stratified whatever its salt'. ENVELOPE: unshifted (scramble zero) only; the pseudorandom-shift leg above is the sibling statement for that axis, and the two are not composed with each other here | — | — | — |

The exception type is compared EXACTLY, not by catch clause, so the ArgumentOutOfRangeException rows cannot be satisfied by the ArgumentException base the later gates throw | — | — | — |

ENVELOPE: 2000000 pairs rather than the full-volume 20000000 — every gate is the full-volume threshold, met at reduced volume with margin rather than loosened to fit. Mutation-probed: swapping the Taylor series' exponent (9→6, i.e. e^3 instead of e^4.5) moves the reference band to roughly 4x the true tail and reddens the case with the exact bounds printed; restored before landing. The full-volume statement at the original 20000000 pairs is sampling.gaussian-moments-cdf-tail-at-scale | — | — |

Mutation-probed: shuffling only the first three of the four elements reddens it at 'permutation 0123 occurred 79624 times over 480000 trials, expected 20000 +/- 700'; restored before landing. | scalar.exp2-vs-series | law: Default | classical | — | FixedQ4816.Exp2 — a 128-entry mantissa table indexed by the exponent's top seven fraction bits, a quartic in the residual at Q62, and a round-half-UP right shift by 46 − ⌊exponent⌋ | Oracles.EncloseExp2, which forms 2^u as the product of the ladder factors 2^(2⁻ⁱ) over the fraction's set bits, the ladder built by REPEATED INTEGER SQUARE ROOTS of two with directed rounding — no table, no polynomial. The envelope is DERIVED from the kernel's own two error terms rather than declared as a step: half a raw ULP for the closing round-half-UP narrowing, plus the mantissa's relative error carried up to the result's scale, bounded by 2⁻⁴⁴. That second bound is the quartic's truncation of the exponential series — the omitted tail Σ_{n≥5} (ln2·r)ⁿ/n! is at most 3.85·10⁻¹⁴ at the largest residual r = 511/2¹⁶, and the six Q62 truncations with the table's own rounding add under 10⁻¹⁸ to it. The absolute arm is ATTAINED, not slack: the −17 tie sits exactly half a ULP above its true value, because this is the family's one round-half-UP kernel. ENVELOPE: Subjects.Exp2ExponentRaw folds every sampled raw onto [−20, 47), the whole NON-saturating interior — above 47 the kernel deliberately answers MaxValue, which no envelope around the true value could contain, so that half-open tail is stated by the gate leg instead. RULED, and the correction is the point: this leg used to state a two-regime STEP — 0.75 raw ULP absolute below a true result of 2²⁷, 2⁻⁴⁰ relative above it — which is discontinuous by a factor of ten at the switch and which the kernel breaches over the octave below it, where its own shape crosses three quarters of a ULP at about 2²⁶·⁸. The kernel is not defective there (0.816 raw ULP observed at the worst operand, a relative 9·10⁻¹⁴); the envelope was mis-stated, and the derived form above is strictly tighter than the step it replaces everywhere below 2²⁶ and sixteen times tighter above 2²⁷ | — | — |

| symmetric-solve.apply-refusal-and-symmetry | law: Default | structural | — | PINS THE APPLY FAMILY'S CONTRACT at hand-derived witnesses, deterministically on every run. The Q16 identity matrix applied to a Q16-to-integer vector returns that vector unchanged, which pins the mixed-scale bridge itself. The exchange matrix [[0,1],[1,0]] applied to (1,2) is (2,1): a kernel that read the off-diagonal into only one row would answer (2,0) or (0,1), a defect a swept comparison against an oracle sharing the same symmetric convention could still miss on symmetric draws. And a call whose FIRST component is exactly 2^63 — one past the raw carrier — while its second is representable must refuse with BOTH outputs at zero, never leave the computed first component behind; that is the same stale-output defect symmetric-solve.refusal-leaves-no-stale-output pins for Solve | — | — | — |

No fold: unlike Solve and Invert, Apply has no preconditioning envelope to stay inside, because each component is a sum of two raw products bounded by 2^127 and therefore exact in the sign-plus-UInt128 accumulator at any operand | Oracles.TryApplySymmetric2 — the exact BigInteger sum rounded once against an explicit power-of-two denominator, with no accumulator width anywhere and the tie decided by 2r against d rather than by the subject's own discarded-bit split | — | — |

| symmetric-solve.solve3-vs-bareiss | law: Default | classical | — | FixedSymmetricSolve.TrySolveSymmetric3 (internal) — the refuse/succeed outcome and every solved component, at a caller-chosen output fraction shift, over SymmetricSolveClaims.FoldModerate's roughly-31-bit-magnitude band | Oracles.TryBareissSolveSymmetric3 — fraction-free (Bareiss) Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting in BigInteger, sharing no cofactor (C11..C33), adjugate, or expanded-determinant formula with the subject or with Oracles.TrySolveSymmetric3's own adjugate transcription. This is the primary defence against a shared sign error in any one of the six cofactors, which solve3-vs-oracle and the residual envelope cannot reliably catch. The concrete C13 witness is K=[[-3,-3,-3],[-3,-3,-2],[-3,-2,-3]], rhs=(-1,-2,1): a shared C13 flip returns the wrong vector (1,2,-3) while both older checks pass — the third symmetric-solve validation's Finding 2 | — | — |

| symmetric-solve.solve3-vs-oracle | law: Default | classical | — | FixedSymmetricSolve.TrySolveSymmetric3 (internal) — the refuse/succeed outcome and every solved component, at a caller-chosen output fraction shift, over SymmetricSolveClaims.FoldModerate's roughly-31-bit-magnitude band — the primary exercise of the six-term triple-product determinant's bit budget (k ≤ 41) | Oracles.TrySolveSymmetric3 — the exact BigInteger Cramer's-rule solve (adf − ae² − b²f + 2bce − c²d and its adjugate cofactors), with no intermediate rounding, no wrapping, and no power-of-two preconditioning of any kind: every entry is read at its own raw magnitude, so a defect in the subject's shift target (for example reusing FixedVectorMath.DirectionShift's bit 45) or its widening cannot also appear in the oracle | — | — |
| symmetric-solve.solve3-vs-oracle | law: Default | structural | — | ENVELOPE: same as symmetric-solve.solve2-vs-oracle's second leg — the fold (magnitude at most roughly 2^31, strictly below the 3×3 family's target-plus-one of 2^41) keeps the shared preconditioning shift non-negative, hence lossless, on every draw, so exact agreement is provable; the large-magnitude corner where a lossy downshift introduces bounded rounding is covered by symmetric-solve.solve3-extreme-magnitude-agrees and symmetric-solve.invert-large-magnitude-envelope-refuses instead. 31 bits of moderate-band magnitude is still ample headroom to exercise the six-term determinant's own overflow safety, since the wrong-bit-45 mutation (see the discrimination record) reaches well past Int128 even at this fold | — | — | — |

The member is INTERNAL, so coverage-manifest.json cannot name it and the ratchet could not notice its only gate being deleted; it is reached here through Puck.Maths.Tests' InternalsVisibleTo and no public member is credited, because none is called | Oracles.NearestIntegerRoot of the exact BigInteger sum of squares - a bracketed integer search whose predicate is one exact squaring, forming no square root at all. This is an EXACT IDENTITY at every swept direction, not a tolerance: whichever branch runs, the returned magnitude IS the nearest integer root rather than a value inside a measured ULP band | — | — |

ENVELOPE: the two tangent2 checks are skipped for an operand whose normal magnitude sits below one raw Q16 unit or above three-quarters of the FixedQ4816 carrier's own magnitude. Below: Cross(tangent1, normal)'s fused-rounding error is bounded in ABSOLUTE raw units, but a small normal has few significant bits to begin with, so that fixed absolute error becomes a much larger ANGULAR error once tangent2 is normalized back to unit length — tangent1 carries no such dependency, which is why only the tangent2 checks are gated. ## Register: shared-substrate statements with no independent leg beside them

What the filter selects, exactly: every shared-substrate leg on a statement that declares no independent leg. It is
NOT a list of owed third legs, and reading it as one contradicts two of this contract's own rules. A
**delegation-twin** or a **transcription** owes no third leg at all — one body read twice cannot be separated by an
operand sweep — and is discharged by its CITATION instead. A **fused-substrate** row is the one that wants an exact
recomputation of the rounding, at operands where the two disciplines genuinely differ. Some rows also say in their
OWN text that the gap is inert: unit operands only, an interior gap that cannot exist, two routes that cannot
differ. No machine can read that, so they are listed anyway and their leg text is the ruling. The gap column keeps
the two fix queues apart.

## Register: legs that mark their own owed work

Every leg whose citation opens `OWED:`, of any kind. The register above keys on the SHAPE of a declaration, so
it cannot see a leg that names a hole in its own envelope: an INDEPENDENT leg admitting one is invisible to it.
This register keys on the marker instead, which is why the marker is the spelling: a leg that opens its citation
`OWED:` lands here whatever kind it is.

| statement | surface | leg kind | subject | the marked gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

## Register: behaviour pinned as observed against its own XML doc

Every leg spelled `Leg.PinnedAsObserved`, whose citation opens `DOC GAP:`. A law that pins what a kernel DOES
where its own documentation says otherwise is legitimate — the alternative is a law tuned to prose — but only while
the divergence is carried somewhere a reader can act on it. This register is that somewhere, derived from the
declarations rather than written beside them, so a leg can neither cite a register that does not exist nor sit in
one that has gone stale. Each row is a decision owed to whoever owns the kernel: correct the code, or correct the
doc. Neither the value nor the doc is blessed by appearing here.

| statement | surface | what the run pins | what the doc claims |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

## Register: transcriptions and the witnesses beside them

A transcription carries a rule the subject's own code already carries, so agreement proves FAITHFUL CARRIAGE and
never that the rule is right — a shared error cancels. Condition (C) forbids counting one as independent evidence,
and the type system enforces it: `Leg.FaithfulCarriage` is shared-substrate, so no transcription can satisfy a
check that demands an independent leg. The witness column is what DOES stand beside it; where it opens `NONE`,
the row is owed one and says so.

not a row here, while a relative statement made inside a claim body is. Every case running
